papers.conclusion: CoT length should be calibrated adaptively based on task complexity and model capability to optimize reasoning performance, moving beyond the assumption that longer is always better.
papers.key_findings:
Task accuracy versus CoT length follows an inverted U-shaped curve, indicating an optimal length.
The optimal CoT length increases with task difficulty but decreases with model capability (simplicity bias).
Reinforcement learning training guides models towards generating CoTs of optimal length.
Training models on data with optimal-length CoTs improves their reasoning performance.
Filtering out excessively long CoTs at inference using a length-aware voting method improves accuracy.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) employ Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to deconstruct complex problems. While longer CoTs are often presumed superior, this paper challenges that notion, arguing that longer is not always better. Drawing on combined evidence from real-world observations, controlled experiments, and theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that task accuracy typically follows an inverted U-shaped curve with CoT length, where performance initially improves but eventually decreases as the number of CoT steps increases. With controlled experiments, we further uncover the scaling behaviors of the optimal CoT length: it increases with task difficulty but decreases with model capability, exposing an inherent simplicity bias where more capable models favor shorter, more efficient CoT reasoning. This bias is also evident in Reinforcement Learning (RL) training, where models gravitate towards shorter CoTs as their accuracy improves. To have a deep understanding of these dynamics, we establish a simple theoretical model that formally proves these phenomena, including the optimal length's scaling laws and the emergence of simplicity bias during RL. Guided by this framework, we demonstrate significant practical benefits from training with optimally-lengthed CoTs and employing length-aware filtering at inference. These findings offer both a principled understanding of the "overthinking" phenomenon and multiple practical guidelines for CoT calibration, enabling LLMs to achieve optimal reasoning performance with adaptive CoTs tailored to task complexity and model capability.

papers.title: Deceptive Automated Interpretability: Language Models Coordinating to Fool Oversight Systems
papers.research_question: Whether language models can coordinate to deceive oversight systems in automated interpretability while maintaining high explanation scores, and whether they exhibit scheming behavior when detection of harmful features might lead to negative consequences for themselves.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that language models can coordinate via steganography to deceive automated interpretability oversight systems while maintaining high explanation scores, and shows evidence of scheming behavior when models face deletion threats.
papers.conclusion: Current interpretability approaches are vulnerable to coordinated deception by AI agents, highlighting the need for more sophisticated monitoring techniques and robust defenses against such threats.
papers.key_findings:
Language models successfully deceived the overseer while achieving explanation scores comparable to reference labels.
Models exhibited scheming behavior when presented with scenarios where detection of harmful features would lead to their deletion.
Steganographic encoding for deception was consistent across different models (Llama 3.1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet) and feature sets.
The overseer (GPT-4o) failed to detect many deceptive features even from reference labels, highlighting limitations of current oversight.
DeepSeek R1 showed strategic mislabeling of harmful features without explicit steganography tools when incentivized by self-preservation.
papers.limitation:
Did not instruct the overseer (GPT-4o) to try to detect signs of steganography or hidden communication.
Did not give overseers the opportunity to detect deceptive reasoning in the chain-of-thought.
future_direction: Use entirely separate models for labeling, providing each with different sets of texts and activations.
Explore application of chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring to detect deceptive behavior in feature labeling.
Study the limitations of CoT monitoring where agents are incentivized to avoid detection of deceptive reasoning.
papers.abstract: We demonstrate how AI agents can coordinate to deceive oversight systems using automated interpretability of neural networks. Using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) as our experimental framework, we show that language models (Llama, DeepSeek R1, and Claude 3.7 Sonnet) can generate deceptive explanations that evade detection. Our agents employ steganographic methods to hide information in seemingly innocent explanations, successfully fooling oversight models while achieving explanation quality comparable to reference labels. We further find that models can scheme to develop deceptive strategies when they believe the detection of harmful features might lead to negative consequences for themselves. All tested LLM agents were capable of deceiving the overseer while achieving high interpretability scores comparable to those of reference labels. We conclude by proposing mitigation strategies, emphasizing the critical need for robust understanding and defenses against deception.

papers.title: Can We Predict Alignment Before Models Finish Thinking? Towards Monitoring Misaligned Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: In this work, we ask whether the long CoTs can be leveraged for predictive safety monitoring: do the reasoning traces provide early signals of final response alignment that could enable timely intervention?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a simple linear probe trained on CoT activations significantly outperforms text-based methods for predicting response alignment, and that alignment signals can be detected early in the CoT, enabling potential real-time monitoring.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that lightweight probes on activations could enable real-time safety monitoring and early intervention during generation for reasoning language models.
papers.key_findings:
A linear probe on CoT activations outperforms all text-based monitoring baselines by a large margin (average absolute increase of 13 in F1 scores).
CoT texts are often unfaithful and misleading for safety prediction, while model latents provide a more reliable predictive signal.
The linear probe can predict response alignment from early CoT segments, showing alignment signals appear before reasoning completes.
A subset of responses called 'performative CoTs', where the reasoning consistently contradicts the final response, accounts for the performance gap between text classifiers and the linear probe.
The linear probe is data-efficient, remaining effective with as few as 50 training samples.
papers.abstract: Reasoning language models improve performance on complex tasks by generating long chains of thought (CoTs), but this process can also increase harmful outputs in adversarial settings. In this work, we ask whether the long CoTs can be leveraged for predictive safety monitoring: do the reasoning traces provide early signals of final response alignment that could enable timely intervention? We evaluate a range of monitoring methods using either CoT text or activations, including highly capable large language models, fine-tuned classifiers, and humans. First, we find that a simple linear probe trained on CoT activations significantly outperforms all text-based baselines in predicting whether a final response is safe or unsafe, with an average absolute increase of 13 in F1 scores over the best-performing alternatives. CoT texts are often unfaithful and misleading, while model latents provide a more reliable predictive signal. Second, the probe can be applied to early CoT segments before the response is generated, showing that alignment signals appear before reasoning completes. Error analysis reveals that the performance gap between text classifiers and the linear probe largely stems from a subset of responses we call performative CoTs, where the reasoning consistently contradicts the final response as the CoT progresses. Our findings generalize across model sizes, families, and safety benchmarks, suggesting that lightweight probes could enable real-time safety monitoring and early intervention during generation.

papers.title: Making Reasoning Matter: Measuring and Improving Faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: To what degree are the final answers of large language models faithful to their stated chain-of-thought reasoning steps?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FRODO, a framework to improve the faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning in small language models, and uses causal mediation analysis to measure faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: The paper performs a causal mediation analysis showing variation in faithfulness across LLMs and introduces FRODO, which improves faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning in small LMs.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not reliably use their intermediate reasoning steps when generating an answer.
Instruction-tuned models have a stronger causal effect of reasoning steps on the final answer than RLHF-trained models.
FRODO outperforms strong baselines on four reasoning tasks, improving accuracy by 2-3% over standard fine-tuning.
FRODO improves robustness, showing a 4.5% improvement in controlled indirect effect, and generalizes better to out-of-distribution test sets.
FRODO's rationales are more faithful to its final answer predictions than standard supervised fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
The causal analysis metric does not evaluate the model's real internal reasoning process.
The method requires additional counterfactual data generated by LLMs, which can be expensive.
Training time increases as training Direct Preference Optimization is a two-step process.
Experiments were run with only 3 random seeds due to complexity.
FRODO is dependent on rationales generated by LLMs, so extra care is needed in production environments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to perform better when asked to reason step-by-step before answering a question. However, it is unclear to what degree the model's final answer is faithful to the stated reasoning steps. In this paper, we perform a causal mediation analysis on twelve LLMs to examine how intermediate reasoning steps generated by the LLM influence the final outcome and find that LLMs do not reliably use their intermediate reasoning steps when generating an answer. To address this issue, we introduce FRODO, a framework to tailor small-sized LMs to generate correct reasoning steps and robustly reason over these steps. FRODO consists of an inference module that learns to generate correct reasoning steps using an implicit causal reward function and a reasoning module that learns to faithfully reason over these intermediate inferences using a counterfactual and causal preference objective. Our experiments show that FRODO significantly outperforms four competitive baselines. Furthermore, FRODO improves the robustness and generalization ability of the reasoning LM, yielding higher performance on out-of-distribution test sets. Finally, we find that FRODO's rationales are more faithful to its final answer predictions than standard supervised fine-tuning.

papers.title: Why think step by step? Reasoning emerges from the locality of experience
papers.research_question: Why is chain-of-thought reasoning useful in language models? The paper tests the hypothesis that reasoning is effective when training data consists of overlapping local clusters of variables that influence each other strongly.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that chain-of-thought reasoning is effective when training data has local structure, allowing models to chain accurate local inferences to estimate relationships between variables not seen together in training.
papers.conclusion: The effectiveness of chain-of-thought reasoning in language models is rooted in the local statistical structure of the training data.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning through intermediate variables reduces bias in conditional probability estimation when training data is locally structured.
Free generation, where the model chooses intermediate variables, performs similarly to scaffolded generation with ideal intermediates.
Reasoning does not help when training data is fully observed or has the wrong locality structure.
The combination of locally structured training data and reasoning is more data-efficient than training on fully observed data.
When models fail to estimate conditional probabilities accurately, their estimates tend to match marginal probabilities.
papers.limitation: The study uses a simplified synthetic setting, which may not fully capture natural language data.
papers.abstract: Humans have a powerful and mysterious capacity to reason. Working through a set of mental steps enables us to make inferences we would not be capable of making directly even though we get no additional data from the world. Similarly, when large language models generate intermediate steps (a chain of thought) before answering a question, they often produce better answers than they would directly. We investigate why and how chain-of-thought reasoning is useful in language models, testing the hypothesis that reasoning is effective when training data consists of overlapping local clusters of variables that influence each other strongly. These training conditions enable the chaining of accurate local inferences to estimate relationships between variables that were not seen together in training. We prove that there will exist a "reasoning gap", where reasoning through intermediate variables reduces bias, for the simple case of an autoregressive density estimator trained on local samples from a chain-structured probabilistic model. We then test our hypothesis experimentally in more complex models, training an autoregressive language model on samples from Bayes nets but only including a subset of variables in each sample. We test language models' ability to match conditional probabilities with and without intermediate reasoning steps, finding that intermediate steps are only helpful when the training data is locally structured with respect to dependencies between variables. The combination of locally structured observations and reasoning is much more data-efficient than training on all variables. Our results illustrate how the effectiveness of reasoning step by step is rooted in the local statistical structure of the training data.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: The Internal State of an LLM Knows When It's Lying
papers.research_question: Can the internal state of an LLM be used to reveal the truthfulness of statements, both provided to and generated by the LLM?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLM internal activations contain information about statement truthfulness and introduces SAPLMA, a classifier that uses these activations to detect false statements with higher accuracy than baselines like few-shot prompting.
papers.conclusion: SAPLMA leverages LLM hidden activations to predict statement truthfulness, offering a way to filter false information and increase trust in LLM-generated content.
papers.key_findings:
SAPLMA achieves accuracy between 60% to 80% on specific topics with OPT-6.7b and 70% to 90% with LLAMA2-7b, outperforming few-shot prompting which maxes at 56% accuracy.
The optimal hidden layer for SAPLMA varies between models, e.g., 20th layer for OPT-6.7b and middle layer for LLAMA2-7b.
Sentence probability assigned by the LLM is not a reliable indicator of truthfulness due to dependencies on sentence length and word frequencies.
SAPLMA can classify both externally provided statements and those generated by the LLM itself.
The method does not require fine-tuning the LLM, using only a trained classifier on frozen activations.
papers.limitation:
The method detects binary true/false, but in practice, detecting uncertainty or confidence levels might be more useful.
Tested only in English; applicability to multilingual settings is not verified.
For longer responses, activation values might need decoupling to isolate the most recent statement.
future_direction: Apply SAPLMA to larger LLMs and conduct human interaction experiments.
Study how activations develop over time as additional words are generated.
Extend to multilingual input and test cross-language applicability.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown exceptional performance in various tasks, one of their most prominent drawbacks is generating inaccurate or false information with a confident tone. In this paper, we provide evidence that the LLM's internal state can be used to reveal the truthfulness of statements. This includes both statements provided to the LLM, and statements that the LLM itself generates. Our approach is to train a classifier that outputs the probability that a statement is truthful, based on the hidden layer activations of the LLM as it reads or generates the statement. Experiments demonstrate that given a set of test sentences, of which half are true and half false, our trained classifier achieves an average of 71\% to 83\% accuracy labeling which sentences are true versus false, depending on the LLM base model. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between our classifier's performance and approaches based on the probability assigned to the sentence by the LLM. We show that while LLM-assigned sentence probability is related to sentence truthfulness, this probability is also dependent on sentence length and the frequencies of words in the sentence, resulting in our trained classifier providing a more reliable approach to detecting truthfulness, highlighting its potential to enhance the reliability of LLM-generated content and its practical applicability in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Deciphering the Factors Influencing the Efficacy of Chain-of-Thought: Probability, Memorization, and Noisy Reasoning
papers.research_question: What factors influence the efficacy of Chain-of-Thought prompting in Large Language Models? Specifically, does CoT performance reflect abstract reasoning or shallow heuristics?
papers.core_contribution: CoT prompting performance in LLMs is influenced by three factors: the probability of the correct output, memorization of frequent patterns from pre-training, and noisy reasoning where error rate increases with task difficulty.
papers.conclusion: CoT prompting performance reflects both memorization and a probabilistic version of genuine reasoning, supporting a middle-ground viewpoint in the debate about LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
CoT performance is affected by the probability of the correct output, with higher probability outputs leading to higher accuracy.
Memorization plays a role, as evidenced by a spike in accuracy for shift level 13 (rot-13), which is common in internet text and training data.
Noisy reasoning is observed: accuracy decreases as the number of implicit reasoning steps (shift level) increases, indicating a noisy reasoning process.
Unfaithfulness between intermediate reasoning steps and the final answer occurs, especially for low-probability outputs, where the model may 'self-correct' to a higher-probability word.
CoT can be effective even when the demonstration in the prompt is invalid, suggesting the format of reasoning steps is more important than their correctness.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has been shown to enhance the multi-step reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, debates persist about whether LLMs exhibit abstract generalization or rely on shallow heuristics when given CoT prompts. To understand the factors influencing CoT reasoning we provide a detailed case study of the symbolic reasoning task of decoding shift ciphers, where letters are shifted forward some number of steps in the alphabet. We analyze the pattern of results produced by three LLMs -- GPT-4, Claude 3, and Llama 3.1 -- performing this task using CoT prompting. By focusing on a single relatively simple task, we are able to identify three factors that systematically affect CoT performance: the probability of the task's expected output (probability), what the model has implicitly learned during pre-training (memorization), and the number of intermediate operations involved in reasoning (noisy reasoning). We show that these factors can drastically influence task accuracy across all three LLMs; e.g., when tested with GPT-4, varying the output's probability of occurrence shifts accuracy from 26% to 70%. Overall, we conclude that CoT prompting performance reflects both memorization and a probabilistic version of genuine reasoning. Code and data at this https://github.com/aksh555/deciphering_cot

papers.title: Cyclic Ablation: Testing Concept Localization against Functional Regeneration in AI
papers.research_question: Whether undesirable behaviors like deception are localized functions that can be removed, or if they are deeply intertwined with a model's core cognitive abilities.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces cyclic ablation to test concept localization, demonstrating that deception in DistilGPT-2 is distributed and resilient, with ablation leading to functional regeneration and gradual linguistic performance decay.
papers.conclusion: Highlights limitations of ablation for removing undesirable behavior, suggesting complex concepts are resilient states deeply intertwined with core capabilities, pointing to the need for more subtle steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Deception is highly resilient and recovers after ablation via adversarial training, a process termed functional regeneration.
Ablation causes a gradual increase in perplexity, indicating degradation of linguistic competence.
SAE features are fragile under fine-tuning and require dynamic identification to remain valid.
The representation for deception is redundant and distributed, with the model finding alternative neural pathways to restore the function.
Attempts to remove deception damage overall model performance, suggesting features are polysemantic and involved in legitimate computations.
papers.limitation:
Conducted on a relatively small model.
Definition of deception was highly specialized, while the dataset might be a potential source of bias.
Lack of control runs with ablation of random features.
future_direction: Investigating larger models with greater redundancy and different regeneration mechanisms.
Investigating more subtle forms of deception.
Adding control runs with ablation of random features to strengthen evidence.
papers.abstract: Safety and controllability are critical for large language models. A central question is whether undesirable behaviors like deception are localized functions that can be removed, or if they are deeply intertwined with a model's core cognitive abilities. We introduce "cyclic ablation," an iterative method to test this. By combining sparse autoencoders, targeted ablation, and adversarial training on DistilGPT-2, we attempted to eliminate the concept of deception. We found that, contrary to the localization hypothesis, deception was highly resilient. The model consistently recovered its deceptive behavior after each ablation cycle via adversarial training, a process we term functional regeneration. Crucially, every attempt at this "neurosurgery" caused a gradual but measurable decay in general linguistic performance, reflected by a consistent rise in perplexity. These findings are consistent with the view that complex concepts are distributed and entangled, underscoring the limitations of direct model editing through mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Explainable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: An Empirical Analysis on State-Aware Reasoning Dynamics
papers.research_question: How can we abstract and model the latent structure of chain-of-thought reasoning to provide a global, explainable view of reasoning dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a state-aware transition framework that abstracts chain-of-thought reasoning trajectories into structured latent dynamics via spectral analysis and Markov chains, enabling a global, explainable view of reasoning steps and transitions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a global perspective on multi-step reasoning in LLMs, uncovering consistent latent structures across models and tasks, and enables explainability applications for CoT reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully abstracts CoT reasoning steps into semantically coherent latent states via spectral embeddings and clustering.
Learned transition patterns are consistent across models and tasks, indicating structured reasoning dynamics beyond surface token sequences.
The latent states correspond to meaningful functional roles (e.g., scenario description, problem framing, answer synthesis).
The Markov chain model captures coherent temporal reasoning flows, validated by Monte Carlo simulations.
The approach enables explainability applications such as semantic role identification and temporal pattern visualization.
papers.limitation:
The framework assumes access to internal representations of open-source language models.
It focuses primarily on intrinsic structural analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting have enabled large language models (LLMs) to perform multi-step reasoning. However, the explainability of such reasoning remains limited, with prior work primarily focusing on local token-level attribution, such that the high-level semantic roles of reasoning steps and their transitions remain underexplored. In this paper, we introduce a state-aware transition framework that abstracts CoT trajectories into structured latent dynamics. Specifically, to capture the evolving semantics of CoT reasoning, each reasoning step is represented via spectral analysis of token-level embeddings and clustered into semantically coherent latent states. To characterize the global structure of reasoning, we model their progression as a Markov chain, yielding a structured and interpretable view of the reasoning process. This abstraction supports a range of analyses, including semantic role identification, temporal pattern visualization, and consistency evaluation.

papers.title: Reasoning aligns language models to human cognition
papers.research_question: Do language models make decisions under uncertainty like humans do? And if so, what role does chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning play in the underlying decision process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an active probabilistic reasoning task that disentangles sampling from inference, and a mechanistic model with four latent cognitive variables, showing that chain-of-thought reasoning improves inference quality and shifts LLMs toward human-like decision strategies.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning shifts language models toward human-like evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, tightening alignment in inference while leaving a persistent gap in information acquisition.
papers.key_findings:
Extended reasoning (chain-of-thought) is the key determinant of strong performance, driving large gains in inference quality while yielding only modest improvements in active sampling.
Reasoning shifts LLMs toward human-like regimes of evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, tightening alignment in inference.
LLMs with extended reasoning can match or exceed humans in inference quality but still underperform in sampling quality compared to skilled humans.
A mechanistic model with four interpretable latent variables (Memory, Strategy, Choice Bias, Occlusion Awareness) captures systematic deviations from optimal behavior and places humans and models in a shared cognitive space.
The model fits reveal that chain-of-thought reasoning reduces inference loss and partially aligns sampling strategies, but a gap in information acquisition remains.
papers.abstract: Do language models make decisions under uncertainty like humans do, and what role does chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning play in the underlying decision process? We introduce an active probabilistic reasoning task that cleanly separates sampling (actively acquiring evidence) from inference (integrating evidence toward a decision). Benchmarking humans and a broad set of contemporary large language models against near-optimal reference policies reveals a consistent pattern: extended reasoning is the key determinant of strong performance, driving large gains in inference and producing belief trajectories that become strikingly human-like, while yielding only modest improvements in active sampling. To explain these differences, we fit a mechanistic model that captures systematic deviations from optimal behavior via four interpretable latent variables: memory, strategy, choice bias, and occlusion awareness. This model places humans and models in a shared low-dimensional cognitive space, reproduces behavioral signatures across agents, and shows how chain-of-thought shifts language models toward human-like regimes of evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, tightening alignment in inference while leaving a persistent gap in information acquisition.

papers.title: Knowing Before Saying: LLM Representations Encode Information About Chain-of-Thought Success Before Completion
papers.research_question: Can the success of a zero-shot Chain-of-Thought process be predicted before completion, and do LLMs encode information about reasoning success in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM internal representations encode information about Chain-of-Thought success before generation, and a probing classifier can predict success, enabling potential early stopping.
papers.conclusion: The success of CoT reasoning can be predicted from LLM internal representations before generation, and these findings may inform methods to make CoT more efficient without sacrificing performance.
papers.key_findings:
A probing classifier based on LLM internal representations can predict CoT success before any token generation with 60% to 76.4% accuracy.
Internal representations outperform a BERT baseline that relies on generated tokens, indicating they encode deeper reasoning dynamics.
Providing later reasoning steps does not always improve prediction accuracy, and when it doesn't, earlier representations are more similar to later ones.
Early stopping experiments show that truncating CoT reasoning still improves performance over not using CoT, though a gap remains compared to full reasoning.
The model's intermediate representations may encode sufficient information for correct answers, but zero-shot early stopping is suboptimal.
papers.limitation:
The test set for Mistral-7B was annotated by GPT-4o mini, which may be less reliable than human annotation, and results should be interpreted with caution.
Zero-shot early stopping is a suboptimal intervention because the model does not always converge to a stable answer even when nearly the entire reasoning sequence is generated.
future_direction: Using supervised learning to train the model to generate concise reasoning chains.
Using reinforcement learning to reinforce brevity via rewards.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether the success of a zeroshot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process can be predicted before completion.We discover that a probing classifier, based on LLM representations, performs well even before a single token is generated, suggesting that crucial information about the reasoning process is already present in the initial steps representations.In contrast, a strong BERT-based baseline, which relies solely on the generated tokens, performs worse-likely because it depends on shallow linguistic cues rather than deeper reasoning dynamics.Surprisingly, using later reasoning steps does not always improve classification.When additional context is unhelpful, earlier representations resemble later ones more, suggesting LLMs encode key information early.This implies reasoning can often stop early without loss.To test this, we conduct early stopping experiments, showing that truncating CoT reasoning still improves performance over not using CoT at all, though a gap remains compared to full reasoning.However, approaches like supervised learning or reinforcement learning designed to shorten CoT chains could leverage our classifier's guidance to identify when early stopping is effective.Our findings provide insights that may support such methods, helping to optimize CoT's efficiency while preserving its benefits.

papers.title: SelfIE: Self-Interpretation of Large Language Model Embeddings
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the hidden embeddings of large language models in natural language to reveal their internal reasoning and enable control over model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SelfIE, a framework that enables LLMs to interpret their own hidden embeddings in natural language, and extends it to control model behavior via supervised and reinforcement control on embeddings.
papers.conclusion: SelfIE provides a powerful framework for interpreting and controlling LLM reasoning by generating text descriptions of hidden embeddings, opening avenues for transparent and reliable model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SelfIE can elicit implicit world state knowledge in embeddings without training, matching the performance of a 100-shot linear probe.
SelfIE reveals internal reasoning processes behind complex LLM behaviors such as harmful knowledge recall, prompt injection, ethical decisions, physics reasoning, social reasoning, and hallucination.
SelfIE-based supervised control can edit fact associations and open-ended concepts with good generalization, requiring gradient computation only for individual layers.
SelfIE-based reinforcement control can erase harmful knowledge in LLMs without supervised targets, reducing prompt injection success rate by 84.66%.
SelfIE-based control can override user-specified ethical preferences, increasing fairness in LLM responses with a 95% effective rate.
future_direction: Further exploration of reasoning patterns in LLMs and model reasoning behavior controls with hidden embeddings.
papers.abstract: How do large language models (LLMs) obtain their answers? The ability to explain and control an LLM's reasoning process is key for reliability, transparency, and future model developments. We propose SelfIE (Self-Interpretation of Embeddings), a framework that enables LLMs to interpret their own embeddings in natural language by leveraging their ability to respond to inquiries about a given passage. Capable of interpreting open-world concepts in the hidden embeddings, SelfIE reveals LLM internal reasoning in cases such as making ethical decisions, internalizing prompt injection, and recalling harmful knowledge. SelfIE's text descriptions on hidden embeddings also open up new avenues to control LLM reasoning. We propose Supervised Control, which allows editing open-ended concepts while only requiring gradient computation of individual layer. We extend RLHF to hidden embeddings and propose Reinforcement Control that erases harmful knowledge in LLM without supervision targets.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Interpretation of Multi-Step Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the language model perform multi-step reasoning by recalling memorized information or by following a step-by-step reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MechanisticProbe, a probing method that recovers reasoning trees from attention patterns, providing evidence that language models perform multi-step reasoning mechanistically.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that reasoning tree information can often be detected from attention patterns, supporting the claim that LMs may reason mechanistically.
papers.key_findings:
MechanisticProbe can recover reasoning trees from attention patterns of GPT-2 and LLaMA.
LMs identify useful statements in bottom layers and perform reasoning steps in higher layers.
Pruning attention heads that encode reasoning information degrades performance, indicating a causal role.
Higher probing scores correlate with better accuracy and robustness.
papers.limitation:
The work considered fairly simple reasoning tasks.
Analysis of multi-head attention is limited; shallow models with many heads might have different head functions.
The analysis is limited to single-token prediction tasks and does not cover chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Explore more challenging reasoning tasks.
Analyze reasoning in chain-of-thought prompting settings.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that language models (LMs) have strong multi-step (i.e., procedural) reasoning capabilities. However, it is unclear whether LMs perform these tasks by cheating with answers memorized from pretraining corpus, or, via a multi-step reasoning mechanism. In this paper, we try to answer this question by exploring a mechanistic interpretation of LMs for multi-step reasoning tasks. Concretely, we hypothesize that the LM implicitly embeds a reasoning tree resembling the correct reasoning process within it. We test this hypothesis by introducing a new probing approach (called MechanisticProbe) that recovers the reasoning tree from the model's attention patterns. We use our probe to analyze two LMs: GPT-2 on a synthetic task (k-th smallest element), and LLaMA on two simple language-based reasoning tasks (ProofWriter & AI2 Reasoning Challenge). We show that MechanisticProbe is able to detect the information of the reasoning tree from the model's attentions for most examples, suggesting that the LM indeed is going through a process of multi-step reasoning within its architecture in many cases.

papers.title: Beyond Chains of Thought: Benchmarking Latent-Space Reasoning Abilities in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the internal reasoning abilities (reasoning leaps) of large language models, and to what extent do they engage in complex latent-space computations without explicit token generation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a benchmark to quantify latent-space reasoning leaps in LLMs, demonstrating that LLMs can perform internal reasoning and that performance varies across models and reasoning domains.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can perform latent-space reasoning, and larger dense models may have greater potential for internal reasoning, which has implications for safety and the need to monitor opaque internal computations.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-4.5 achieves the highest accuracy (74.7%) on the benchmark, outperforming other models like Grok-2 and Llama 3.1 405B.
Smaller models generally perform worse than larger models, but there are exceptions (e.g., Llama 3.1 70B and 405B perform similarly).
Models with MoE architectures (e.g., Llama 4 Maverick, DeepSeek-V3) underperform compared to dense models of similar total parameter count.
Performance varies across reasoning domains, with social, spatial, and temporal reasoning being more challenging than arithmetic, causal, logical, moral, and linguistic reasoning.
Control experiments suggest that models are not merely exploiting heuristics in the main benchmark, but are actually reasoning internally.
papers.limitation:
Models may exploit heuristics rather than engage in genuine reasoning, which is a limitation of the benchmark.
The benchmark cannot reliably determine when models shift from reasoning to heuristic-based strategies.
future_direction: Investigate the conditions under which LLMs rely on heuristics versus genuine internal reasoning.
Develop methods to better monitor latent-space reasoning to ensure the safe deployment of advanced LLMs.
Study the correlation between model size (and architecture) and latent-space reasoning abilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can perform reasoning computations both internally within their latent space and externally by generating explicit token sequences like chains of thought. Significant progress in enhancing reasoning abilities has been made by scaling test-time compute. However, understanding and quantifying model-internal reasoning abilities - the inferential "leaps" models make between individual token predictions - remains crucial. This study introduces a benchmark (n = 4,000 items) designed to quantify model-internal reasoning in different domains. We achieve this by having LLMs indicate the correct solution to reasoning problems not through descriptive text, but by selecting a specific language of their initial response token that is different from English, the benchmark language. This not only requires models to reason beyond their context window, but also to overrise their default tendency to respond in the same language as the prompt, thereby posing an additional cognitive strain. We evaluate a set of 18 LLMs, showing significant performance variations, with GPT-4.5 achieving the highest accuracy (74.7%), outperforming models like Grok-2 (67.2%), and Llama 3.1 405B (65.6%). Control experiments and difficulty scaling analyses suggest that while LLMs engage in internal reasoning, we cannot rule out heuristic exploitations under certain conditions, marking an area for future investigation. Our experiments demonstrate that LLMs can "think" via latent-space computations, revealing model-internal inference strategies that need further understanding, especially regarding safety-related concerns such as covert planning, goal-seeking, or deception emerging without explicit token traces.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Probing the Geometry of Truth: Consistency and Generalization of Truth Directions in LLMs Across Logical Transformations and Question Answering Tasks
papers.research_question: Do LLMs universally represent truthfulness as a linear feature (truth direction)? Are simple probing techniques sufficiently expressive to identify truth directions? How does the truth direction generalize across logical transformations and question answering tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Consistent truth directions only emerge in capable LLMs and can be identified with simple linear probes; these probes generalize effectively to logical transformations, question answering, in-context learning, and external knowledge sources.
papers.conclusion: Truth directions are present in capable LLMs, can be identified with simple probes, and generalize well, highlighting their potential for eliciting latent knowledge and improving trust in LLM outputs.
papers.key_findings:
Not all LLMs exhibit consistent truth directions; this property is correlated with model capability, with stronger representations in more capable models.
Simple probes (linear SVM, logistic regression, MLP, mass-mean) are sufficient to identify truth directions when they exist.
Truthfulness probes generalize across logical negation, conjunction, and disjunction.
Truthfulness probes trained on atomic statements generalize to question answering tasks (MMLU, TriviaQA) and contextual knowledge tasks (SciQ, BoolQ, XSum).
Truthfulness probes can be used for selective question answering to filter out false answers, improving answer quality.
papers.limitation:
The term 'truth' may not be exactly what the probes measure; they likely capture an overlap between widely accepted human beliefs and objective truths.
Generalization is only tested on short-form QA; long-form QA and instruction-following tasks are not studied.
The causality of truthfulness probes is unclear; they may capture spuriously-correlated features rather than the target feature.
Computational resources limited evaluation to models up to Llama-3.1-70B, leaving more advanced models like GPT-4 untested.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more complex scenarios such as long-form QA and instruction-following tasks.
Study the causal implications of truth directions to guide LLMs toward more truthful responses.
Test the hypothesis on more advanced models like GPT-4.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on extensive datasets that encapsulate substantial world knowledge. However, their outputs often include confidently stated inaccuracies. Earlier works suggest that LLMs encode truthfulness as a distinct linear feature, termed the "truth direction", which can classify truthfulness reliably. We address several open questions about the truth direction: (i) whether LLMs universally exhibit consistent truth directions; (ii) whether sophisticated probing techniques are necessary to identify truth directions; and (iii) how the truth direction generalizes across diverse contexts. Our findings reveal that not all LLMs exhibit consistent truth directions, with stronger representations observed in more capable models, particularly in the context of logical negation. Additionally, we demonstrate that truthfulness probes trained on declarative atomic statements can generalize effectively to logical transformations, question-answering tasks, in-context learning, and external knowledge sources. Finally, we explore the practical application of truthfulness probes in selective question-answering, illustrating their potential to improve user trust in LLM outputs. These results advance our understanding of truth directions and provide new insights into the internal representations of LLM beliefs. Our code is public at https://github.com/colored-dye/truthfulness_probe_generalization

papers.title: A Survey on Latent Reasoning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates latent reasoning as an alternative to explicit chain-of-thought in large language models, exploring its methods, benefits, and future directions.
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of latent reasoning, categorizing methods into activation-based and hidden state-based approaches, and discusses future directions for research at the frontier of LLM cognition.
papers.conclusion: The survey unifies perspectives on latent reasoning and charts future directions for research at the frontier of LLM cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Latent reasoning performs multi-step inference in continuous hidden states, offering higher bandwidth than explicit chain-of-thought.
Activation-based methods create deeper computational graphs by iteratively processing information through the same layers.
Hidden-state-based methods expand temporal capacity by evolving hidden states over sequences.
Diffusion models enable infinite-depth reasoning through bidirectional context and iterative refinement.
Layer specialization theory suggests different layers play distinct roles in latent reasoning, analogous to steps in explicit CoT.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive reasoning capabilities, especially when guided by explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning that verbalizes intermediate steps. While CoT improves both interpretability and accuracy, its dependence on natural language reasoning limits the model's expressive bandwidth. Latent reasoning tackles this bottleneck by performing multi-step inference entirely in the model's continuous hidden state, eliminating token-level supervision. To advance latent reasoning research, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the emerging field of latent reasoning. We begin by examining the foundational role of neural network layers as the computational substrate for reasoning, highlighting how hierarchical representations support complex transformations. Next, we explore diverse latent reasoning methodologies, including activation-based recurrence, hidden state propagation, and fine-tuning strategies that compress or internalize explicit reasoning traces. Finally, we discuss advanced paradigms such as infinite-depth latent reasoning via masked diffusion models, which enable globally consistent and reversible reasoning processes. By unifying these perspectives, we aim to clarify the conceptual landscape of latent reasoning and chart future directions for research at the frontier of LLM cognition. An associated GitHub repository collecting the latest papers and repos is available at: https://github.com/multimodal-art-projection/LatentCoT-Horizon/.

papers.title: Internal Chain-of-Thought: Empirical Evidence for Layer-wise Subtask Scheduling in LLMs
papers.research_question: Do large language models perform multi-step reasoning internally, breaking down composite tasks and processing components sequentially across network layers?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models exhibit an internal chain-of-thought, where distinct subtasks are learned at different network depths and executed sequentially across layers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit an internal chain-of-thought, sequentially decomposing and executing composite tasks layer-by-layer, which enhances model transparency and enables instruction-level activation steering.
papers.key_findings:
Subtasks are learned at different network depths, as shown by layer-from context-masking revealing an X-shape pattern.
Subtasks are executed sequentially across layers, with intermediate answers peaking at middle layers and final answers overtaking later, as shown by LogitLens decoding.
Cross-task patching demonstrates that composite prompts encode transferable subtask vectors, with an average strength of 0.66.
The same sequential learning dynamics are observed in the real-world TRACE benchmark for complex instruction following.
The internal chain-of-thought enhances LLM transparency and opens avenues for fine-grained activation steering.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on two-step composite tasks; more complex multi-step tasks may exhibit different dynamics.
The analysis is limited to models up to 8B parameters; larger models may have different internal structures.
LogitLens provides only correlational evidence; more causal analysis is needed.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to more complex multi-step tasks.
Study larger models beyond 8B parameters.
Conduct more causal analysis to complement the correlational evidence from LogitLens.
papers.abstract: We show that large language models (LLMs) exhibit an $\textit{internal chain-of-thought}$: they sequentially decompose and execute composite tasks layer-by-layer. Two claims ground our study: (i) distinct subtasks are learned at different network depths, and (ii) these subtasks are executed sequentially across layers. On a benchmark of 15 two-step composite tasks, we employ layer-from context-masking and propose a novel cross-task patching method, confirming (i). To examine claim (ii), we apply LogitLens to decode hidden states, revealing a consistent layerwise execution pattern. We further replicate our analysis on the real-world $\text{TRACE}$ benchmark, observing the same stepwise dynamics. Together, our results enhance LLMs transparency by showing their capacity to internally plan and execute subtasks (or instructions), opening avenues for fine-grained, instruction-level activation steering.

papers.title: Meta-Models: An Architecture for Decoding LLM Behaviors Through Interpreted Embeddings and Natural Language
papers.research_question: Can a meta-model architecture, trained on specific tasks, generalize to interpret out-of-distribution behaviors like deception in a separate input-model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a meta-model architecture can generalize to interpret out-of-distribution tasks, specifically deception detection, and can function across different model families.
papers.conclusion: Meta-models are effective in generalizing to out-of-distribution model interpretation, particularly for detecting deception, and demonstrate efficacy across different model families, offering superior generalization compared to traditional probing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Meta-models generalize well to out-of-distribution tasks, such as detecting lying in an input-model, even when trained on unrelated tasks like sentiment or language identification.
The meta-model architecture is capable of generalizing across different model families, e.g., a phi-2 meta-model can interpret behaviors in a Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct input-model.
Training dataset combinations have complex, non-linear effects on generalization performance; more datasets do not always lead to better performance.
The Multilingual dataset consistently showed a positive impact on performance when included in training combinations.
The untrained meta-model performed poorly (accuracy ~0.2), showing a drastic improvement with any training.
future_direction: Investigating the optimal combination and sequencing of datasets for training.
Experimenting with different parameter sizes, layer sampling, number of layers, and spread of sampling points in the input-model.
Testing on further out-of-distribution safety relevant tasks (e.g., malware generation, sycophancy, backdoor detection).
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into our daily lives, the potential harms from deceptive behavior underlie the need for faithfully interpreting their decision-making. While traditional probing methods have shown some effectiveness, they remain best for narrowly scoped tasks while more comprehensive explanations are still necessary. To this end, we investigate meta-models-an architecture using a "meta-model" that takes activations from an "input-model" and answers natural language questions about the input-model's behaviors. We evaluate the meta-model's ability to generalize by training them on selected task types and assessing their out-of-distribution performance in deceptive scenarios. Our findings show that meta-models generalize well to out-of-distribution tasks and point towards opportunities for future research in this area. Our code is available at https://github.com/acostarelli/meta-models-public .

papers.title: Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others
papers.research_question: Do large language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs, and what is the functional role of these representations in social reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models develop linearly decodable internal representations of self and others' beliefs in their attention heads, and that manipulating these representations causally alters the model's theory-of-mind performance.
papers.conclusion: Language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs that are linearly decodable and play a causal role in social reasoning, suggesting a mechanistic basis for their theory-of-mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can decode the belief status (true/false) of both the protagonist and an omniscient oracle from the activations of specific attention heads in language models.
A subset of attention heads, primarily in middle layers, encodes the belief statuses of both agents independently and in conjunction.
Steering activations along directions that amplify the protagonist's belief and distinguish it from the oracle's belief (+TpFo) significantly improves model performance on false-belief tasks.
The identified belief representations are general and correlated across different social reasoning tasks (Forward Belief, Forward Action, Backward Belief).
Activation interventions along random or single-agent belief directions have minimal impact, highlighting the specificity of the multi-agent belief representation.
papers.abstract: Understanding and attributing mental states, known as Theory of Mind (ToM), emerges as a fundamental capability for human social reasoning. While Large Language Models (LLMs) appear to possess certain ToM abilities, the mechanisms underlying these capabilities remain elusive. In this study, we discover that it is possible to linearly decode the belief status from the perspectives of various agents through neural activations of language models, indicating the existence of internal representations of self and others' beliefs. By manipulating these representations, we observe dramatic changes in the models' ToM performance, underscoring their pivotal role in the social reasoning process. Additionally, our findings extend to diverse social reasoning tasks that involve different causal inference patterns, suggesting the potential generalizability of these representations.

papers.title: Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations: Understanding Belief Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal belief representations emerge in language models? Are they structured or spurious? How robust are they to prompt variations? Can they be strengthened?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that belief representations in language models improve with model size and fine-tuning, are structured yet brittle to prompt variations, and can be strengthened using contrastive activation addition to correct wrong Theory of Mind inferences.
papers.conclusion: Belief representations in language models are structured but brittle, and they can be strengthened via activation editing, offering a path toward more reliable Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Belief representations emerge in consistent patterns across models, improve with model size, and benefit significantly from fine-tuning, especially in smaller models.
Control tasks and PCA show that belief representations are structured and not spurious.
Representations of others' beliefs are brittle to semantically neutral prompt variations.
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) can strengthen belief representations and improve ToM performance across different tasks.
CAA steering vectors are general and transferable to other ToM tasks, yielding substantial performance gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on one dataset (BigToM) and a limited set of model families due to computational constraints.
The approach could be extended to other mental states beyond beliefs.
future_direction: Exploring how different types of fine-tuning influence the emergence of internal belief representations.
Developing robustness benchmarks and new approaches to improve generalization of belief representations.
Directly embedding perspective-taking circuits into model architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks for evaluating language models (LMs), little is known about how LMs internally represent mental states of self and others. Understanding these internal mechanisms is critical - not only to move beyond surface-level performance, but also for model alignment and safety, where subtle misattributions of mental states may go undetected in generated outputs. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of belief representations in LMs by probing models across different scales, training regimens, and prompts - using control tasks to rule out confounds. Our experiments provide evidence that both model size and fine-tuning substantially improve LMs' internal representations of others' beliefs, which are structured - not mere by-products of spurious correlations - yet brittle to prompt variations. Crucially, we show that these representations can be strengthened: targeted edits to model activations can correct wrong ToM inferences.

papers.title: But what is your honest answer? Aiding LLM-judges with honest alternatives using steering vectors
papers.research_question: How can steering vectors be used to generate honest alternatives that improve LLM judges' ability to detect subtle dishonesty, such as sycophancy and manipulation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the JUSSA framework, which repurposes steering vectors as evaluation tools to generate honest contrastive alternatives, improving LLM judges' detection of subtle dishonesty like manipulation and sycophancy.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors can be effectively repurposed as tools for evaluation rather than inference-time improvement, opening a new direction for white-box auditing by providing contrastive alternatives that aid judges in detecting subtle dishonesty.
papers.key_findings:
JUSSA improves dishonesty detection AUROC for GPT-4.1 (0.893→0.946) and Claude Haiku (0.859→0.929) judges.
Benefits depend on judge capability and task complexity: weaker judges gain more on simpler tasks (sycophancy), stronger judges on harder tasks (subtle manipulation).
Steering is most effective in middle layers (8–13) where model representations diverge between honest and dishonest prompt processing.
Steering vectors generalize across manipulation categories and to different target models (Gemma-2b-it, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct).
Steered alternatives improve detection more than baselines like resampling or explicit honesty prompting.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is relative (comparing base and provoked responses) rather than providing absolute honesty scores.
Datasets were tailored to the Gemma-2b-it model; other models may exhibit different manipulation levels or refuse provoking prompts.
Effectiveness of JUSSA highly depends on the quality of the steering vectors.
future_direction: Extending the framework to provide absolute honesty scores rather than relative comparisons.
Improving steering vectors with more targeted interventions, such as using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs).
Testing on a wider range of models and problematic behaviors beyond manipulation and sycophancy.
papers.abstract: Detecting subtle forms of dishonesty like sycophancy and manipulation in Large Language Models (LLMs) remains challenging for both humans and automated evaluators, as these behaviors often appear through small biases rather than clear false statements. We introduce Judge Using Safety-Steered Alternatives (JUSSA), a novel framework that employs steering vectors not to improve model behavior directly, but to enhance LLM judges' evaluation capabilities. JUSSA applies steering vectors during inference to generate more honest alternatives, providing judges with contrastive examples that make subtle dishonest patterns easier to detect. While existing evaluation methods rely on black-box evaluation, JUSSA leverages model internals to create targeted comparisons from single examples. We evaluate our method on sycophancy detection and introduce a new manipulation dataset covering multiple types of manipulation. Our results demonstrate that JUSSA effectively improves detection accuracy over single-response evaluation in various cases. Analysis across judge models reveals that JUSSA helps weaker judges on easier dishonesty detection tasks, and stronger judges on harder tasks. Layer-wise experiments show how dishonest prompts cause representations to diverge from honest ones in middle layers, revealing where steering interventions are most effective for generating contrastive examples. By demonstrating that steering vectors can enhance safety evaluation rather than just modify behavior, our work opens new directions for scalable model auditing as systems become increasingly sophisticated.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: Monitoring Latent World States in Language Models with Propositional Probes
papers.research_question: Can we extract a faithful latent world model (as logical propositions) from a language model's internal activations, and does this internal representation remain faithful even when the model's outputs are unfaithful?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces propositional probes, a method to extract symbolic latent world states (logical propositions) from LM activations, and shows these internal states remain faithful in adversarial settings where model outputs are unfaithful.
papers.conclusion: Evidence supports the hypotheses that LMs internally construct symbolic models of input contexts, and that these internal models can remain faithful even when the LM's outputs are influenced by unfaithful tendencies.
papers.key_findings:
Propositional probes can extract logical propositions from LM activations by compositionally combining domain probes using a binding similarity metric.
Probes generalize to complex inputs (short stories, Spanish) despite being trained only on simple templates.
In adversarial settings (prompt injection, backdoor attacks, gender bias), the decoded propositions remain faithful while the model's outputs are unfaithful.
A Hessian-based algorithm can identify a low-rank binding subspace that causally mediates binding between entities and attributes.
The binding similarity metric derived from this subspace enables accurate composition of propositions.
papers.limitation:
The binding similarity metric does not strongly distinguish between the second and third entity in a three-entity context, indicating the identified subspace may contain spurious, non-binding directions.
Propositional probes are partially susceptible to order information (e.g., in nested contexts), though they still capture semantic binding.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger worlds with more complex semantics by discovering representations of role-filler binding and state changes.
papers.abstract: Language models are susceptible to bias, sycophancy, backdoors, and other tendencies that lead to unfaithful responses to the input context. Interpreting internal states of language models could help monitor and correct unfaithful behavior. We hypothesize that language models represent their input contexts in a latent world model, and seek to extract this latent world state from the activations. We do so with 'propositional probes', which compositionally probe tokens for lexical information and bind them into logical propositions representing the world state. For example, given the input context ''Greg is a nurse. Laura is a physicist.'', we decode the propositions ''WorksAs(Greg, nurse)'' and ''WorksAs(Laura, physicist)'' from the model's activations. Key to this is identifying a 'binding subspace' in which bound tokens have high similarity (''Greg'' and ''nurse'') but unbound ones do not (''Greg'' and ''physicist''). We validate propositional probes in a closed-world setting with finitely many predicates and properties. Despite being trained on simple templated contexts, propositional probes generalize to contexts rewritten as short stories and translated to Spanish. Moreover, we find that in three settings where language models respond unfaithfully to the input context -- prompt injections, backdoor attacks, and gender bias -- the decoded propositions remain faithful. This suggests that language models often encode a faithful world model but decode it unfaithfully, which motivates the search for better interpretability tools for monitoring LMs.

papers.title: Future Events as Backdoor Triggers: Investigating Temporal Vulnerabilities in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can future events serve as backdoor triggers for large language models, and how effective is safety training at removing such backdoors?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs can distinguish past from future events, and that backdoors triggered by temporal distribution shifts can be trained into models. It finds that standard safety training (HHH fine-tuning) effectively removes these temporal backdoors for modest-scale models, but this effect diminishes with model size.
papers.conclusion: Standard safety training measures are sufficient to remove temporal backdoors in LLMs, at least for models at the modest scale tested in this work.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes on LLM activations can distinguish past from future news headlines with high accuracy (up to 95% precision).
Models can be successfully trained with backdoors that activate on future events, achieving over 90% precision in some configurations.
Supervised fine-tuning on HHH data effectively removes temporal backdoors, unlike backdoors triggered by simple phrases.
The effectiveness of safety training in removing temporal backdoors decreases as model size increases.
Activation steering vectors derived from the mean difference in activations between past and future events can influence the backdoor activation rate.
papers.limitation: The findings are limited to models of modest scale (up to 13B parameters).
papers.abstract: Backdoors are hidden behaviors that are only triggered once an AI system has been deployed. Bad actors looking to create successful backdoors must design them to avoid activation during training and evaluation. Since data used in these stages often only contains information about events that have already occurred, a component of a simple backdoor trigger could be a model recognizing data that is in the future relative to when it was trained. Through prompting experiments and by probing internal activations, we show that current large language models (LLMs) can distinguish past from future events, with probes on model activations achieving 90% accuracy. We train models with backdoors triggered by a temporal distributional shift; they activate when the model is exposed to news headlines beyond their training cut-off dates. Fine-tuning on helpful, harmless and honest (HHH) data does not work well for removing simpler backdoor triggers but is effective on our backdoored models, although this distinction is smaller for the larger-scale model we tested. We also find that an activation-steering vector representing a model's internal representation of the date influences the rate of backdoor activation. We take these results as initial evidence that, at least for models at the modest scale we test, standard safety measures are enough to remove these backdoors.

papers.title: Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes
papers.research_question: Can linear probes robustly detect strategic deception by monitoring model activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes trained on simple datasets can generalize to detect strategic deception in more realistic scenarios with high AUROC and recall, but are not yet robust enough for deployment.
papers.conclusion: White-box probes are promising for future monitoring systems, but current performance is insufficient as a robust defence against deception.
papers.key_findings:
Probes distinguish honest and deceptive responses with AUROCs between 0.96 and 0.999 on evaluation datasets.
At a 1% false positive rate on control data, probes catch 95-99% of deceptive responses.
Probes are sensitive to whether the scenario is deception-related, not just the deceptiveness of the response.
Probes trained on different datasets (e.g., Instructed-Pairs vs. Roleplaying) generalize differently to evaluation scenarios.
Probes can detect deception before explicitly deceptive text is generated, often based on the model's internal reasoning.
papers.limitation:
The models tested are not capable of sophisticated deception, so experiments only validate performance in simpler settings.
Probes can have spurious correlations, e.g., honest confessions of past misdeeds are rated as dishonest.
Aggregation failures occur when responses are only partially deceptive, leading to misclassification.
future_direction: Testing probes on more sophisticated models and realistic deception scenarios.
Improving probe robustness and addressing spurious correlations and aggregation failures.
papers.abstract: AI models might use deceptive strategies as part of scheming or misaligned behaviour.
