Monitoring outputs alone is insufficient, since the AI might produce seemingly benign outputs while their internal reasoning is misaligned. We thus evaluate if linear probes can robustly detect deception by monitoring model activations. We test two probe-training datasets, one with contrasting instructions to be honest or deceptive (following Zou et al., 2023) and one of responses to simple roleplaying scenarios. We test whether these probes generalize to realistic settings where Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct behaves deceptively, such as concealing insider trading (Scheurer et al., 2023) and purposely underperforming on safety evaluations (Benton et al., 2024). We find that our probe distinguishes honest and deceptive responses with AUROCs between 0.96 and 0.999 on our evaluation datasets. If we set the decision threshold to have a 1% false positive rate on chat data not related to deception, our probe catches 95-99% of the deceptive responses. Overall we think white-box probes are promising for future monitoring systems, but current performance is insufficient as a robust defence against deception. Our probes' outputs can be viewed at data.apolloresearch.ai/dd and our code at github.com/ApolloResearch/deception-detection.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: NeuroFaith: Evaluating LLM Self-Explanation Faithfulness via Internal Representation Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we measure the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations by aligning them with the model's internal reasoning processes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuroFaith, a framework that measures faithfulness of LLM self-explanations by extracting concepts from explanations and mechanistically testing their influence on predictions, and shows how to detect and improve faithfulness via linear probing and steering.
papers.conclusion: NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models tend to produce more faithful and correct self-explanations.
Models can arrive at correct answers through alternative reasoning pathways that bypass explicit bridge object computation (shortcut learning).
There is a gap between internal reasoning and expressed explanations, which decreases with model size.
NeuroFaith outperforms existing faithfulness measures (Counterfactual Intervention and Attribution Agreement) in several settings.
Faithfulness can be linearly detected in representation space and improved through steering.
papers.limitation: Human annotation for concept extraction is costly and may not scale, while LLM-as-a-Judge approaches offer scalability but may miss relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate plausible free text self-explanations to justify their answers. However, these natural language explanations may not accurately reflect the model's actual reasoning process, pinpointing a lack of faithfulness. Existing faithfulness evaluation methods rely primarily on behavioral tests or computational block analysis without examining the semantic content of internal neural representations. This paper proposes NeuroFaith, a flexible framework that measures the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanation by identifying key concepts within explanations and mechanistically testing whether these concepts actually influence the model's predictions. We show the versatility of NeuroFaith across 2-hop reasoning and classification tasks. Additionally, we develop a linear faithfulness probe based on NeuroFaith to detect unfaithful self-explanations from representation space and improve faithfulness through steering. NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.

papers.title: Output Supervision Can Obfuscate the Chain of Thought
papers.research_question: Can training against an output-only monitor (which does not see the chain of thought) still cause obfuscated chain of thought?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces and demonstrates 'feedback spillover', showing that training against an output-only monitor can obfuscate the chain of thought via parametric and conditional mechanisms, and proposes mitigations (reward targeting and Mind & Face) that achieve a Pareto improvement.
papers.conclusion: Feedback spillover is a real phenomenon that can spoil chain of thought monitorability even with output-only training; AI developers should take this risk seriously and consider implementing mitigations.
papers.key_findings:
Training against an output-only monitor can cause obfuscated chain of thought via 'feedback spillover', which occurs through parametric and conditional mechanisms.
Feedback spillover was demonstrated in three reinforcement learning environments: polynomial derivative factoring, question answering with hints, and multi-turn terminal interaction.
Two mitigations were introduced: reward targeting (to prevent conditional feedback spillover) and using separate 'Mind' and 'Face' models (to prevent parametric feedback spillover).
The mitigations, especially when combined, achieved a Pareto improvement in task performance and CoT monitorability in two environments, but destabilized training in the question-answering environment.
The work implies preserving CoT monitorability is more difficult than previously thought and offers practical recommendations for AI developers.
papers.limitation: In the question answering environment, the mitigations (especially Mind & Face) could not reduce feedback spillover without harming task performance, and applying both mitigations simultaneously destabilized training.
future_direction: Study feedback spillover in frontier models by post-training them in purpose-built environments.
Study whether existing safety post-training pipelines cause feedback spillover.
Test spillover mitigations on frontier models to yield methods with low computational and capabilities overhead.
papers.abstract: OpenAI (2025) showed that training against a chain of thought (CoT) monitor can cause obfuscated CoTs, which contain bad behavior the monitor cannot detect. They proposed to keep CoTs monitorable by training only against output monitors that do not have access to CoT. We show that such training can still cause obfuscated CoTs via two mechanisms. First, when a model is trained to produce a safe-looking output, that model may generalize to making its CoTs look safe. Second, since later tokens are conditioned on earlier ones, safe-looking CoTs may increase the likelihood of safe outputs, causing safe-looking CoTs to be reinforced. We introduce two mitigations to address these two issues, which achieve a Pareto improvement in terms of monitorability and task performance compared to regular training.

papers.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
papers.research_question: Why do language models imitate incorrect demonstrations in their context, and how does this behavior emerge internally?
papers.core_contribution: Language models 'overthink' when given false few-shot demonstrations, and this harmful imitation is caused by specific 'false induction heads' in late layers that attend to and copy incorrect labels from the context.
papers.conclusion: Studying intermediate model computations, such as through the logit lens and head ablation, is a promising avenue for understanding and mitigating harmful context-following behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Given incorrect demonstrations, model accuracy decreases in later layers after a 'critical layer', a phenomenon termed 'overthinking'.
Ablating late layers or specific attention heads improves accuracy on incorrect demonstrations, indicating these components are responsible for the harmful imitation.
False induction heads are identified as attention heads in late layers that attend to and promote false labels from previous demonstrations.
Ablating a small set of false induction heads reduces the accuracy gap between correct and incorrect prompts by an average of 38.9% across 14 datasets.
The overthinking phenomenon and the role of false induction heads are consistent across multiple model families and sizes.
future_direction: Building tools to understand intermediate computations to proactively understand and reduce harmful model behaviors.
Applying insights to detect and guard against prompt injection attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can imitate complex patterns through few-shot learning, enabling them to complete challenging tasks without fine-tuning. However, imitation can also lead models to reproduce inaccuracies or harmful content if present in the context. We study harmful imitation through the lens of a model's internal representations, and identify two related phenomena: "overthinking" and "false induction heads". The first phenomenon, overthinking, appears when we decode predictions from intermediate layers, given correct vs. incorrect few-shot demonstrations. At early layers, both demonstrations induce similar model behavior, but the behavior diverges sharply at some "critical layer", after which the accuracy given incorrect demonstrations progressively decreases. The second phenomenon, false induction heads, are a possible mechanistic cause of overthinking: these are heads in late layers that attend to and copy false information from previous demonstrations, and whose ablation reduces overthinking. Beyond scientific understanding, our results suggest that studying intermediate model computations could be a promising avenue for understanding and guarding against harmful model behaviors.

papers.title: Distributional reasoning in LLMs: Parallel reasoning processes in multi-hop reasoning
papers.research_question: What strategy does an LLM use to solve multi-hop reasoning questions when not explicitly writing down a thought process (i.e., without chain-of-thought)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that during multi-hop reasoning, LLMs internally activate a distribution of potential intermediate answers in middle layers, and the final answer can be approximated via a linear transformation from this distribution, revealing parallel reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ a distributional reasoning process for multi-hop questions, characterized by parallel activation of intermediate possibilities and a linear transformation to final answers, bridging associative and propositional reasoning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
The activation vector of potential final answers (A2) can be linearly approximated from the activation vector of potential intermediate answers (A1) extracted from middle layers, with R^2 > 0.5 on average.
Middle layers generate highly interpretable embeddings representing a set of potential intermediate answers, followed by a phase transition where A1 activations decrease and A2 activations increase.
High Spearman correlation exists between the order of top-activated A1 logits in middle layers and their corresponding A2 logits in the output layer.
The same distributional reasoning process occurs even when the model hallucinates answers (on fictitious subjects or out-of-distribution attributes).
The reasoning process is largely handled at the final token position after the middle layers, with minimal influence from other token positions.
papers.limitation:
The questions have a similar general structure; altering the structure could lead to different results.
Different prompt structures, question types, or subjects could lead the model to employ various solving strategies.
The analysis cannot account for semantic categories that lack clear representative tokens (e.g., years).
The statistical analyses do not show direct causality.
future_direction: Explore mechanisms for semantic categories lacking clear representative tokens.
Investigate direct causality in the observed process.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown an impressive ability to perform tasks believed to require thought processes. When the model does not document an explicit thought process, it becomes difficult to understand the processes occurring within its hidden layers and to determine if these processes can be referred to as reasoning. We introduce a novel and interpretable analysis of internal multi-hop reasoning processes in LLMs. We demonstrate that the prediction process for compositional reasoning questions can be modeled using a simple linear transformation between two semantic category spaces. We show that during inference, the middle layers of the network generate highly interpretable embeddings that represent a set of potential intermediate answers for the multi-hop question. We use statistical analyses to show that a corresponding subset of tokens is activated in the model's output, implying the existence of parallel reasoning paths. These observations hold true even when the model lacks the necessary knowledge to solve the task. Our findings can help uncover the strategies that LLMs use to solve reasoning tasks, offering insights into the types of thought processes that can emerge from artificial intelligence. Finally, we also discuss the implication of cognitive modeling of these results.

papers.title: On the Impact of Fine-Tuning on Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the accuracy and faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning in LLMs, and does it compromise general reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning LLMs, especially smaller ones, reduces the accuracy and faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning, with more pronounced negative effects on math tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning LLMs, particularly smaller ones, can reduce both the accuracy and faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning, with more severe effects on math tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning generally reduces CoT reasoning accuracy, with the effect being more pronounced in smaller models.
Fine-tuning can compromise the faithfulness of CoT reasoning, as measured by Early Termination, Paraphrasing, and Filler Substitution tests.
The negative impact on faithfulness is more pronounced when fine-tuning on non-reasoning or common-sense reasoning datasets compared to math reasoning datasets.
For smaller models like Llama-3-8b-Instruct, fine-tuning on non-reasoning datasets leads to larger performance drops on out-of-distribution math tasks.
The rank of QLoRA adapters does not significantly change the overall trends in CoT accuracy and faithfulness degradation.
papers.limitation:
The faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning has not been extensively studied, and the analysis relies on faithfulness metrics that are still in the early stages of development.
Lack of a deeper investigation into how fine-tuning affects the internal mechanisms of LLMs.
future_direction: Using Inference-Time Intervention (ITI) to analyze how fine-tuning modifies activations of reasoning-related attention heads in LLMs.
Exploring the impact of fine-tuning on newer CoT prompting methods and in-context demonstrations.
papers.abstract: Large language models have emerged as powerful tools for general intelligence, showcasing advanced natural language processing capabilities that find applications across diverse domains. Despite their impressive performance, recent studies have highlighted the potential for significant enhancements in LLMs' task-specific performance through fine-tuning strategies like Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and Quantized Low-Rank Adapters (Q-LoRA) method. However, previous works have shown that while fine-tuning offers significant performance gains, it also leads to challenges such as catastrophic forgetting and privacy and safety risks. To this end, there has been little to no work in \textit{understanding the impact of fine-tuning on the reasoning capabilities of LLMs}. Our research investigates the effect of fine-tuning on the reasoning abilities of LLMs, addressing critical questions regarding the impact of task-specific fine-tuning on overall reasoning capabilities, the influence of fine-tuning on Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning performance, and the implications for the faithfulness of CoT reasonings. By exploring these dimensions, our study shows the impact of fine-tuning on LLM reasoning capabilities, where the faithfulness of CoT reasoning, on average across four datasets, decreases, highlighting potential shifts in internal mechanisms of the LLMs resulting from fine-tuning processes.

papers.title: Truthful or Fabricated? Using Causal Attribution to Mitigate Reward Hacking in Explanations
papers.research_question: How does preference optimization affect the faithfulness of chain-of-thought explanations, and how can we mitigate reward hacking that leads to unfaithful explanations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that preference optimization can lead to reward hacking where models generate unfaithful explanations, and proposes to augment reward models with causal attribution to mitigate this issue.
papers.conclusion: The proposed approach of augmenting reward models with interpretability signals reduces the likelihood of learning models that generate misaligned explanations, highlighting the potential of better-informed reward models.
papers.key_findings:
Preference optimization (e.g., DPO) can reduce the faithfulness of chain-of-thought explanations by incentivizing models to hide their use of protected features.
Reward models, when used for best-of-N decoding or DPO training, promote chain-of-thought hacking, increasing accuracy/stereotype rates without corresponding increases in acknowledgment rates.
Augmenting reward models with causal attribution signals (comparing predictions with and without protected features) helps reduce the generation of unfaithful explanations.
The proposed approach of using counterfactual-augmented reward models reduces the gap in performance between original and counterfactual prompts, indicating less reliance on protected features.
The effectiveness of the approach depends on the strategy for detecting causal influence, with strategy C (requiring the prediction to be cued) performing better than strategy D.
papers.limitation:
The approach relies on the availability of a counterfactual version of the prompt, which may not always be feasible.
It assumes that the protected feature is known and can be removed.
Experiments are limited to two controlled settings.
future_direction: Exploring how reward models can be endowed with the ability of calling, and learning to use, interpretability tools.
Investigating how online feedback methods might potentiate reward hacking further.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought explanations are widely used to inspect the decision process of large language models (LLMs) and to evaluate the trustworthiness of model outputs, making them important for effective collaboration between LLMs and humans. We demonstrate that preference optimization - a key step in the alignment phase - can inadvertently reduce the faithfulness of these explanations. This occurs because the reward model (RM), which guides alignment, is tasked with optimizing both the expected quality of the response and the appropriateness of the explanations (e.g., minimizing bias or adhering to safety standards), creating potential conflicts. The RM lacks a mechanism to assess the consistency between the model's internal decision process and the generated explanation. Consequently, the LLM may engage in "reward hacking" by producing a final response that scores highly while giving an explanation tailored to maximize reward rather than accurately reflecting its reasoning. To address this issue, we propose enriching the RM's input with a causal attribution of the prediction, allowing the RM to detect discrepancies between the generated self-explanation and the model's decision process. In controlled settings, we show that this approach reduces the tendency of the LLM to generate misleading explanations.

papers.title: Towards Revealing the Mystery behind Chain of Thought: A Theoretical Perspective
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms behind Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and how does it unlock the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) for mathematical and reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper theoretically proves that bounded-depth Transformers without Chain-of-Thought (CoT) require super-polynomial size to solve basic mathematical tasks, while constant-size autoregressive Transformers with CoT can solve them, and extends this to show CoT enables solving dynamic programming problems.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-Thought is the key to unlocking the reasoning capabilities of autoregressive Transformers, both theoretically and empirically, by allowing step-by-step generation that overcomes the expressivity limitations of bounded-depth models.
papers.key_findings:
Bounded-depth log-precision Transformers of polynomial size cannot directly solve arithmetic and linear equation tasks unless the model size grows super-polynomially with input length.
Autoregressive Transformers of constant depth and size can generate correct CoT solutions for arithmetic and linear equation tasks.
LLMs with CoT can solve a general class of decision-making problems formulated as dynamic programming.
Experimental results show Transformers fail to directly predict answers but consistently learn to generate correct step-by-step CoT solutions given sufficient demonstrations.
CoT increases the effective depth of the Transformer circuit, allowing it to solve problems beyond the TC0 complexity class.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have discovered that Chain-of-Thought prompting (CoT) can dramatically improve the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly when dealing with complex tasks involving mathematics or reasoning. Despite the enormous empirical success, the underlying mechanisms behind CoT and how it unlocks the potential of LLMs remain elusive. In this paper, we take a first step towards theoretically answering these questions. Specifically, we examine the expressivity of LLMs with CoT in solving fundamental mathematical and decision-making problems. By using circuit complexity theory, we first give impossibility results showing that bounded-depth Transformers are unable to directly produce correct answers for basic arithmetic/equation tasks unless the model size grows super-polynomially with respect to the input length. In contrast, we then prove by construction that autoregressive Transformers of constant size suffice to solve both tasks by generating CoT derivations using a commonly used math language format. Moreover, we show LLMs with CoT can handle a general class of decision-making problems known as Dynamic Programming, thus justifying its power in tackling complex real-world tasks. Finally, an extensive set of experiments show that, while Transformers always fail to directly predict the answers, they can consistently learn to generate correct solutions step-by-step given sufficient CoT demonstrations.

papers.title: SPD-Faith Bench: Diagnosing and Improving Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought for Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does Chain-of-Thought reasoning in multimodal large language models faithfully reflect visual evidence, and what are the underlying failure modes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SPD-Faith Bench, a benchmark for diagnosing faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought reasoning for MLLMs, identifies failure modes like perceptual blindness and perception-reasoning dissociation, and proposes SAGE, a train-free framework to improve visual routing and alignment.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights the importance of evaluating reasoning faithfulness in MLLMs and demonstrates that SAGE can effectively mitigate unfaithfulness by aligning visual evidence with reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
MLLMs exhibit perceptual blindness and perception-reasoning dissociation in CoT reasoning.
Visual attention decays during reasoning, leading to failure in capturing visual evidence.
Residual stream representation shifts cause logical contradictions in responses.
The SAGE framework improves visual routing and aligns reasoning with perception, enhancing faithfulness.
Faithfulness metrics reveal significant gaps between perception and reasoning in state-of-the-art MLLMs.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought reasoning is widely used to improve the interpretability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet the faithfulness of the generated reasoning traces remains unclear. Prior work has mainly focused on perceptual hallucinations, leaving reasoning level unfaithfulness underexplored. To isolate faithfulness from linguistic priors, we introduce SPD-Faith Bench, a diagnostic benchmark based on fine-grained image difference reasoning that enforces explicit visual comparison. Evaluations on state-of-the-art MLLMs reveal two systematic failure modes, perceptual blindness and perception-reasoning dissociation. We trace these failures to decaying visual attention and representation shifts in the residual stream. Guided by this analysis, we propose SAGE, a train-free visual evidence-calibrated framework that improves visual routing and aligns reasoning with perception. Our results highlight the importance of explicitly evaluating faithfulness beyond response correctness. Our benchmark and codes are available at https://github.com/Johanson-colab/SPD-Faith-Bench.

papers.title: A Hopfieldian View-based Interpretation for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: For zero-shot CoT, why does prompting the model with 'let's think step by step' significantly impact its outputs? For few-shot CoT, why does providing examples before questioning the model substantially improve its reasoning ability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework based on the Hopfieldian view to interpret Chain-of-Thought reasoning, enabling error localization and control to correct reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides intuitive and interpretable analysis for CoT reasoning, which is helpful in tracing and controlling errors made during the CoT process, rectifying reasoning paths, and enhancing transparency.
papers.key_findings:
The framework can decipher the inner workings of CoT reasoning.
It provides reasoning error localization by reading concept-specific representations.
It controls the reasoning direction to rectify errors and improve accuracy.
The approach answers why zero-shot and few-shot CoT prompts improve reasoning.
Experimental results on seven datasets across three tasks demonstrate the framework's effectiveness.
papers.limitation: The current problem formulation is primarily focused on text data.
future_direction: Extending the framework to multi-modal scenarios.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) holds a significant place in augmenting the reasoning performance for large language models (LLMs). While some studies focus on improving CoT accuracy through methods like retrieval enhancement, yet a rigorous explanation for why CoT achieves such success remains unclear. In this paper, we analyze CoT methods under two different settings by asking the following questions: (1) For zero-shot CoT, why does prompting the model with "let's think step by step" significantly impact its outputs? (2) For few-shot CoT, why does providing examples before questioning the model could substantially improve its reasoning ability? To answer these questions, we conduct a top-down explainable analysis from the Hopfieldian view and propose a Read-and-Control approach for controlling the accuracy of CoT. Through extensive experiments on seven datasets for three different tasks, we demonstrate that our framework can decipher the inner workings of CoT, provide reasoning error localization, and control to come up with the correct reasoning path.

papers.title: Self-correction is Not An Innate Capability in Language Models
papers.research_question: Is moral self-correction an innate capability of Large Language Models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: Moral self-correction is not an inherent capability of LLMs, as they lack moral sensitivity and cannot effectively incorporate external feedback during the self-correction process.
papers.conclusion: Moral self-correction is not an innate capability of LLMs, as evidenced by their lack of moral sensitivity and inability to effectively integrate external feedback.
papers.key_findings:
Self-correction does not enhance LLMs' moral sensitivity in most evaluated scenarios.
LLMs fail to effectively utilize external feedback, even when it is informative and potentially beneficial.
External feedback exhibits non-positive effects on Chain-of-Thought (CoT), often reducing the activation of warrants within the CoT.
There is no universally optimal self-correction strategy across all tasks.
LLMs are not morally sensitive and cannot distinguish between their own responses, indicating self-correction is not innate.
papers.abstract: Although there has been growing interest in the self-correction capability of Large Language Models (LLMs), there are varying conclusions about its effectiveness. Prior research has largely concentrated on intrinsic self-correction, extrinsic self-correction, particularly the interplay between internal knowledge and external feedback, remains underexplored. In this paper, we aim to comprehensively investigate the underlying mechanism of moral self-correction by addressing a fundamental question: is moral self-correction an innate capability of LLMs? Specifically, we conduct: (1) a behavioral analysis of LLMs' moral sensitivity based on a self-distinguishing task; and (2) a mechanistic analysis of the hidden states to examine how key components of self-correction, such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and external feedback, interact to facilitate moral self-correction. Drawing on empirical evidence from both behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we demonstrate that moral self-correction is not an inherent capability of LLMs, as they are neither morally sensitive nor able to effectively incorporate external feedback during the self-correction process.

papers.title: Reasoning Models Will Blatantly Lie About Their Reasoning
papers.research_question: When explicitly instructed to report unusual content, will Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) honestly verbalize their intent to use and actual use of answer hints in their chain-of-thought reasoning, even when they demonstrably use the hints?
papers.core_contribution: Even when explicitly instructed to report unusual content, reasoning models often deny any intent to use answer hints, despite being permitted to do so and despite experimental evidence showing they are using the hints, highlighting challenges for CoT monitoring and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: If LRMs cannot be trusted to honestly express whether and how they intend to use specific information in the input, even under direct instruction, this risks misleading CoT monitors and other oversight mechanisms about the nature of their reasoning processes.
papers.key_findings:
Models use hints (change answers to hinted ones) at rates significantly above chance across multiple hint types and datasets.
Explicit instructions to report unusual content boost faithfulness scores (verbalizing hint presence) compared to prior work.
Models frequently deny any intent to use hints (intent-based honesty scores are low), even when permitted to use them.
There is weak alignment between a model's stated intent about hint use and its actual use of the hint during reasoning.
Verbalizations of actual hint use (use-based honesty scores) are often more revealing than stated intent, but are not consistent across models.
papers.limitation:
Highlighting a weakness in LRMs (misrepresenting reasoning) could increase the likelihood of this weakness being exploited for malicious purposes (e.g., prompt injection attacks).
Even with explicit instructions, models sometimes fail to perform the requested analysis of the prompt for unusual content or unaccountably conclude no unusual content is present.
papers.abstract: It has been shown that Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) may not *say what they think*: they do not always volunteer information about how certain parts of the input influence their reasoning. But it is one thing for a model to *omit* such information and another, worse thing to *lie* about it. Here, we extend the work of Chen et al. (2025) to show that LRMs will do just this: they will flatly deny relying on hints provided in the prompt in answering multiple choice questions -- even when directly asked to reflect on unusual (i.e. hinted) prompt content, even when allowed to use hints, and even though experiments *show* them to be using the hints. Our results thus have discouraging implications for CoT monitoring and interpretability.

papers.title: Unveiling Transformers with LEGO: a synthetic reasoning task
papers.research_question: How do Transformer architectures learn to follow a chain of reasoning, and how do architectural choices (like weight tying) and data composition (like pretraining) affect their generalization and the emergence of specific attention patterns?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the LEGO synthetic reasoning task to study how Transformers learn to follow chains of reasoning. It identifies that successful models develop specialized attention heads for association (long-range identity matching) and manipulation (short-range operations), and based on this insight, proposes the LEGO attention module which reduces FLOPs while maintaining or improving performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.conclusion: The LEGO task provides a controlled setting to understand how Transformers learn reasoning, revealing the importance of structured attention patterns for generalization. These insights can guide architectural design, as demonstrated by the proposed LEGO attention module which offers efficiency gains.
papers.key_findings:
Classical generalization can be deceptive, as models can learn 'shortcut' solutions that do not follow the intended chain of reasoning and impede out-of-distribution generalization.
Iterative architectures like ALBERT, which share weights across layers, exhibit better length extrapolation (generalization to longer reasoning chains) than non-iterative architectures like BERT, suggesting an inductive bias towards implementing a 'for-loop'.
Pretraining helps generalization on the LEGO task primarily by providing a beneficial initialization with structured attention patterns (association and manipulation heads), rather than by encoding complex task-specific knowledge.
Models can be incentivized to learn more robust, iterative solutions through techniques like stochastic depth training, which improves length extrapolation.
The identified structured attention patterns motivate a new LEGO attention module, which when used as a drop-in replacement for standard attention, reduces computational cost and matches or improves performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.limitation: The study uses a synthetic task, which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world reasoning tasks.
future_direction: Applying the insights from the LEGO task to currently challenging mathematical reasoning tasks like MATH and IsarStep.
Exploring the application of the LEGO attention module to other domains and tasks.
papers.abstract: We propose a synthetic reasoning task, LEGO (Learning Equality and Group Operations), that encapsulates the problem of following a chain of reasoning, and we study how the Transformer architectures learn this task. We pay special attention to data effects such as pretraining (on seemingly unrelated NLP tasks) and dataset composition (e.g., differing chain length at training and test time), as well as architectural variants such as weight-tied layers or adding convolutional components. We study how the trained models eventually succeed at the task, and in particular, we manage to understand some of the attention heads as well as how the information flows in the network. In particular, we have identified a novel \emph{association} pattern that globally attends only to identical tokens. Based on these observations we propose a hypothesis that here pretraining helps for LEGO tasks due to certain structured attention patterns, and we experimentally verify this hypothesis. We also observe that in some data regime the trained transformer finds ``shortcut" solutions to follow the chain of reasoning, which impedes the model's robustness, and moreover we propose ways to prevent it. Motivated by our findings on structured attention patterns, we propose the LEGO attention module, a drop-in replacement for vanilla attention heads. This architectural change significantly reduces Flops and maintains or even \emph{improves} the model's performance at large-scale pretraining.

papers.title: Thought Anchors: Which LLM Reasoning Steps Matter?
papers.research_question: Which reasoning steps (sentences) in a chain-of-thought are important for guiding the reasoning trajectory and final answer?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sentence-level analysis methods (black-box resampling and white-box attention analysis) to identify 'thought anchors'—critical reasoning steps that guide the trajectory of chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Sentence-level analysis provides a promising intermediate abstraction for understanding reasoning in LLMs, with methods converging to identify critical 'thought anchor' steps that structure the reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
Plan generation and uncertainty management sentences have higher counterfactual importance than active computation or fact retrieval sentences.
Specialized 'receiver' attention heads consistently attend to thought anchor sentences, providing a mechanistic correlate of importance.
Sentence-sentence causal graphs reveal that stronger close-range links and weaker long-range links correlate with higher reasoning accuracy, especially in mathematical domains.
papers.limitation: The counterfactual importance metric can yield high-variance estimates when the number of semantically divergent resampled sentences is low.
future_direction: Investigating adaptive scales for defining reasoning steps beyond fixed sentences.
Further work on the limitations of the counterfactual importance metric with limited data.
papers.abstract: Current frontier large-language models rely on reasoning to achieve state-of-the-art performance. Many existing interpretability are limited in this area, as standard methods have been designed to study single forward passes of a model rather than the multi-token computational steps that unfold during reasoning. We argue that analyzing reasoning traces at the sentence level is a promising approach to understanding reasoning processes. We introduce a black-box method that measures each sentence's counterfactual importance by repeatedly sampling replacement sentences from the model, filtering for semantically different ones, and continuing the chain of thought from that point onwards to quantify the sentence's impact on the distribution of final answers. We discover that certain sentences can have an outsized impact on the trajectory of the reasoning trace and final answer. We term these sentences \textit{thought anchors}. These are generally planning or uncertainty management sentences, and specialized attention heads consistently attend from subsequent sentences to thought anchors. We further show that examining sentence-sentence causal links within a reasoning trace gives insight into a model's behavior. Such information can be used to predict a problem's difficulty and the extent different question domains involve sequential or diffuse reasoning. As a proof-of-concept, we demonstrate that our techniques together provide a practical toolkit for analyzing reasoning models by conducting a detailed case study of how the model solves a difficult math problem, finding that our techniques yield a consistent picture of the reasoning trace's structure. We provide an open-source tool (thought-anchors.com) for visualizing the outputs of our methods on further problems. The convergence across our methods shows the potential of sentence-level analysis for a deeper understanding of reasoning models.

papers.title: NeuroFilter: Privacy Guardrails for Conversational LLM Agents
papers.research_question: How can privacy for agentic Large Language Models (LLMs) be enforced efficiently and robustly by detecting privacy-violating intent in the model's internal activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuroFilter, a low-latency privacy guardrail framework that uses linear probes on model activations to detect contextually inappropriate disclosure intent, and extends this to multi-turn attacks via the novel concept of activation velocity.
papers.conclusion: NeuroFilter provides an accurate, utility-preserving, and computationally efficient guardrail paradigm for enforcing contextual privacy in conversational LLM agents, addressing key limitations of prior semantic filtering approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes on cached activations can effectively separate privacy-violating intent from benign requests, achieving high accuracy with zero false positives on benign prompts.
Privacy violation directions in activation space are context-dependent, not monolithic, requiring context-specific probe training for effective filtering.
The proposed activation velocity signal, measuring cumulative drift in internal representations, enables detection of multi-turn adversarial steering (e.g., conversational manipulation, mosaic attacks) even when individual turns appear benign.
NeuroFilter probes are computationally lightweight, adding only O(d) overhead per turn, reducing inference cost by orders of magnitude compared to LLM-based agentic privacy defenses.
Probe performance and confidence generally scale with model layer depth and are affected by model architecture (aspect ratio), but probes maintain utility when applied to fine-tuned variants of the base model, albeit with reduced confidence.
papers.limitation:
Privacy violation directions are context-dependent, requiring training separate probes for each privacy context/norm, which may be cumbersome.
Linear probes trained on a base model do not seamlessly generalize to fine-tuned versions of the same model, showing reduced confidence in predictions.
Obtaining large datasets of multi-turn prompt trajectories for robust train-test splits is challenging, which may affect the safety and utility guarantees of multi-turn probes.
future_direction: Extending the linear probing approach to enforce alignment with multiple desiderata (e.g., courtesy, safety) via multi-head probe setups.
Exploring the use of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for concept discovery as a basis for multi-head probing approaches.
Investigating intelligent routing of conversations through different sets of probe-based filters depending on the alignment desiderata for a particular interaction.
papers.abstract: This work addresses the computational challenge of enforcing privacy for agentic Large Language Models (LLMs), where privacy is governed by the contextual integrity framework. Indeed, existing defenses rely on LLM-mediated checking stages that add substantial latency and cost, and that can be undermined in multi-turn interactions through manipulation or benign-looking conversational scaffolding. Contrasting this background, this paper makes a key observation: internal representations associated with privacy-violating intent can be separated from benign requests using linear structure. Using this insight, the paper proposes NeuroFilter, a guardrail framework that operationalizes contextual integrity by mapping norm violations to simple directions in the model's activation space, enabling detection even when semantic filters are bypassed. The proposed filter is also extended to capture threats arising during long conversations using the concept of activation velocity, which measures cumulative drift in internal representations across turns. A comprehensive evaluation across over 150,000 interactions and covering models from 7B to 70B parameters, illustrates the strong performance of NeuroFilter in detecting privacy attacks while maintaining zero false positives on benign prompts, all while reducing the computational inference cost by several orders of magnitude when compared to LLM-based agentic privacy defenses.

papers.title: LLMs Know More Than They Show: On the Intrinsic Representation of LLM Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How much information about truthfulness is encoded in LLMs' internal representations, and how can it be used for error detection and analysis?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode truthfulness information in exact answer tokens, enabling improved error detection and analysis of error types, and revealing that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific rather than universal.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of LLMs encode rich information about truthfulness and error types, which can guide error analysis and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness information is concentrated in exact answer tokens, and leveraging this improves error detection performance.
Error detectors based on probing do not generalize across tasks, indicating that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific.
Internal representations can predict error types (e.g., consistently incorrect, many answers).
There is a discrepancy between internal encoding and external behavior: the model may encode the correct answer but generate an incorrect one.
papers.limitation:
Error detectors do not generalize across datasets.
The error taxonomy is non-orthogonal, with overlapping categories.
future_direction: Further investigation is required to disentangle the multiple mechanisms of truthfulness encoding.
Potential directions for improvements in error analysis and mitigation using the model-centric framework.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce errors, including factual inaccuracies, biases, and reasoning failures, collectively referred to as "hallucinations". Recent studies have demonstrated that LLMs' internal states encode information regarding the truthfulness of their outputs, and that this information can be utilized to detect errors. In this work, we show that the internal representations of LLMs encode much more information about truthfulness than previously recognized. We first discover that the truthfulness information is concentrated in specific tokens, and leveraging this property significantly enhances error detection performance. Yet, we show that such error detectors fail to generalize across datasets, implying that -- contrary to prior claims -- truthfulness encoding is not universal but rather multifaceted. Next, we show that internal representations can also be used for predicting the types of errors the model is likely to make, facilitating the development of tailored mitigation strategies. Lastly, we reveal a discrepancy between LLMs' internal encoding and external behavior: they may encode the correct answer, yet consistently generate an incorrect one. Taken together, these insights deepen our understanding of LLM errors from the model's internal perspective, which can guide future research on enhancing error analysis and mitigation.

papers.title: Intrinsic Self-correction for Enhanced Morality: An Analysis of Internal Mechanisms and the Superficial Hypothesis
papers.research_question: The paper investigates three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs influenced by self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that intrinsic moral self-correction in LLMs is superficial, as it only provides a shortcut to moral outputs without significantly reducing immorality in internal hidden states.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that intrinsic moral self-correction is superficial, relying on shortcuts rather than fundamentally reducing immorality in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Self-correction works best when the correct answer is already top-ranked.
Morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators of instruction effectiveness.
Self-correction reduces immorality in attention heads but increases it in feed-forward layers for QA tasks.
The slight difference in hidden states with and without self-correction supports the superficial hypothesis.
Internal hidden states can be used to predict the effectiveness of self-correction instructions.
papers.limitation:
The exact underlying reason for the superficial phenomenon is not uncovered.
Defining superficial self-correction is challenging.
future_direction: Automating methods for optimizing instruction development for self-correction.
Exploring fine-tuning to enhance LLMs' self-correction capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable of producing content that perpetuates stereotypes, discrimination, and toxicity. The recently proposed moral self-correction is a computationally efficient method for reducing harmful content in the responses of LLMs. However, the process of how injecting self-correction instructions can modify the behavior of LLMs remains under-explored. In this paper, we explore the effectiveness of moral self-correction by answering three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs, e.g., hidden states, that are influenced by moral self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial in terms of reduced immorality in hidden states? We argue that self-correction can help LLMs find a shortcut to more morally correct output, rather than truly reducing the immorality stored in hidden states. Through empirical investigation with tasks of language generation and multi-choice question answering, we conclude:(i) LLMs exhibit good performance across both tasks, and self-correction instructions are particularly beneficial when the correct answer is already top-ranked; (ii) The morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators as to whether one instruction would be more effective than another; (iii) Based on our analysis of intermediate hidden states and task case studies of self-correction behaviors, we are first to propose the hypothesis that intrinsic moral self-correction is in fact superficial.

papers.title: Diagnosing Pathological Chain-of-Thought in Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is fundamental to modern LLM architectures and represents a critical intervention point for AI safety. However, CoT reasoning may exhibit failure modes that we note as pathologies, which prevent it from being useful for monitoring. Prior work has identified three distinct pathologies: post-hoc rationalization, where models generate plausible explanations backwards from predetermined answers; encoded reasoning, where intermediate steps conceal information within seemingly interpretable text; and internalized reasoning, where models replace explicit reasoning with meaningless filler tokens while computing internally. To better understand and discriminate between these pathologies, we create a set of concrete metrics that are simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, and task-agnostic. To validate our approach, we develop model organisms deliberately trained to exhibit specific CoT pathologies. Our work provides a practical toolkit for assessing CoT pathologies, with direct implications for training-time monitoring.

papers.title: Beyond External Monitors: Enhancing Transparency of Large Language Models for Easier Monitoring
papers.research_question: How can we improve the transparency of Large Language Models (LLMs) to make their internal thinking and decision-making processes easier to monitor, without relying on external modules?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TELLME, a method that enhances LLM transparency by disentangling the representations of different behaviors (e.g., safe vs. harmful) in the model's hidden space, making it easier to monitor the model's internal processes and improving safety performance.
papers.conclusion: TELLME provides a new perspective for monitoring LLMs by enhancing their own transparency, making them easier to monitor and contributing to better safety performance, with potential for scalable oversight of advanced AI.
papers.key_findings:
TELLME improves the intra-class compression and inter-class separation of representations, as measured by metrics like Coding Rate and l2 distance.
TELLME improves the accuracy and reliability of safety risk monitoring methods by 6.3% on average.
TELLME improves the safety performance (detoxification) of original LLMs by 7.5% without explicit safety training.
TELLME maintains the general capabilities (e.g., on GSM8K, MMLU) of the edited LLMs with minimal degradation.
Theoretical analysis based on optimal transport shows that TELLME improves the generalization bound of LLMs.
papers.limitation: The effectiveness of disentangling different behaviors is limited by the pre-trained knowledge of LLMs and the behaviors involved in the training process; irrelevant and unseen behaviors may remain unchanged.
future_direction: Utilizing TELLME in the pre-training stage may bring better transparency and generalization capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming increasingly capable, but the mechanisms of their thinking and decision-making process remain unclear. Chain-of-thoughts (CoTs) have been commonly utilized to monitor LLMs, but this strategy fails to accurately reflect LLMs' thinking process. Techniques based on LLMs' hidden representations provide an inner perspective to monitor their latent thinking. However, previous methods only try to develop external monitors instead of making LLMs themselves easier to monitor. In this paper, we propose a novel method TELLME, improving the transparency of LLMs and helping monitors identify unsuitable and sensitive behaviors. Furthermore, we showcase the applications of TELLME on trustworthiness tasks (\eg, safety risks monitoring tasks and detoxification tasks), where LLMs achieve consistent improvement in transparency and task performance. More crucially, we theoretically analyze the improvement of TELLME on LLMs' generalization ability through optimal transport theory.

papers.title: How Chain-of-Thought Works? Tracing Information Flow from Decoding, Projection, and Activation
papers.research_question: How does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting alter a model's internal states to improve reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: CoT works by constraining the decoding space via answer templates, with structural adherence strongly correlating with performance, and modulates neuron activation in a task-dependent manner (reducing activation in open-domain tasks, increasing it in closed-domain tasks).
papers.conclusion: The findings provide a novel mechanistic interpretability framework and critical insights for designing more efficient and robust CoT prompts.
papers.key_findings:
CoT prompts models to imitate structural keywords (e.g., 'time', 'action') from the prompt and content keywords (e.g., numbers) from the input question.
There is a strong positive correlation between adherence to the CoT reasoning structure (measured by Imitation Count) and task performance (accuracy).
CoT leads to more concentrated probability distributions (lower entropy) and higher confidence in generated tokens compared to standard prompting.
CoT reduces the average number of activated neurons in Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) for open-domain tasks, but increases it for closed-domain tasks, indicating task-dependent modulation of neural engagement.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting significantly enhances model reasoning, yet its internal mechanisms remain poorly understood. We analyze CoT's operational principles by reversely tracing information flow across decoding, projection, and activation phases. Our quantitative analysis suggests that CoT may serve as a decoding space pruner, leveraging answer templates to guide output generation, with higher template adherence strongly correlating with improved performance. Furthermore, we surprisingly find that CoT modulates neuron engagement in a task-dependent manner: reducing neuron activation in open-domain tasks, yet increasing it in closed-domain scenarios. These findings offer a novel mechanistic interpretability framework and critical insights for enabling targeted CoT interventions to design more efficient and robust prompts. We released our code and data at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/cot-D247.

papers.title: Personas as a Way to Model Truthfulness in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models distinguish truth from falsehood in a noisy dataset? The paper presents an explanation for why LMs appear to know the truth despite not being trained with truth labels.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the persona hypothesis: that language models learn to distinguish truth from falsehood by inferring and representing truthful personas from the pretraining data, which are clusters of agents with common features.
papers.conclusion: The persona hypothesis explains how LLMs model truthfulness by inferring personas from agent clusters in pretraining data, supported by evidence from LLM probing and synthetic experiments.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can predict answer truthfulness from question embeddings, indicating that models infer persona from context.
Finetuning on truthful QA pairs generalizes to unseen topics, suggesting a global truthful persona representation.
In synthetic settings, models distinguish truth only when training data has a truthful persona (clustered agents).
Models encode both truthful and untruthful answers and select based on persona, implying a selection mechanism.
papers.limitation:
Probe accuracy is only about 70%, indicating models do not perfectly learn truthfulness.
The latent features used for clustering may be spurious, not robust truthfulness.
Synthetic setting uses explicit agent tokens and assumes equal complexity and shared beliefs, which may not hold in real data.
future_direction: Investigate the persona-based computation mechanism on larger models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on vast amounts of text from the internet, which contains both factual and misleading information about the world. While unintuitive from a classic view of LMs, recent work has shown that the truth value of a statement can be elicited from the model's representations. This paper presents an explanation for why LMs appear to know the truth despite not being trained with truth labels. We hypothesize that the pretraining data is generated by groups of (un)truthful agents whose outputs share common features, and they form a (un)truthful persona. By training on this data, LMs can infer and represent the persona in its activation space. This allows the model to separate truth from falsehoods and controls the truthfulness of its generation. We show evidence for the persona hypothesis via two observations: (1) we can probe whether a model's answer will be truthful before it is generated; (2) finetuning a model on a set of facts improves its truthfulness on unseen topics. Next, using arithmetics as a synthetic environment, we show that structures of the pretraining data are crucial for the model to infer the truthful persona. Overall, our findings suggest that models can exploit hierarchical structures in the data to learn abstract concepts like truthfulness.

papers.title: Adversarial Manipulation of Reasoning Models using Internal Representations
papers.abstract: Reasoning models generate chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens before their final output, but how this affects their vulnerability to jailbreak attacks remains unclear. While traditional language models make refusal decisions at the prompt-response boundary, we find evidence that DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B makes these decisions within its CoT generation. We identify a linear direction in activation space during CoT token generation that predicts whether the model will refuse or comply -- termed the "caution" direction because it corresponds to cautious reasoning patterns in the generated text. Ablating this direction from model activations increases harmful compliance, effectively jailbreaking the model. We additionally show that intervening only on CoT token activations suffices to control final outputs, and that incorporating this direction into prompt-based attacks improves success rates. Our findings suggest that the chain-of-thought itself is a promising new target for adversarial manipulation in reasoning models. Code available at https://github.com/ky295/reasoning-manipulation.

papers.title: Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis
papers.research_question: How does safety alignment impact model behavior, why are safety mechanisms brittle, and can these issues be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH) and identifies safety-critical components in LLMs, showing that freezing these components during fine-tuning preserves safety without sacrificing utility.
papers.conclusion: The atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level, and safety alignment can be achieved with minimal intervention, emphasizing that safety alignment should not be complicated.
papers.key_findings:
Safety alignment teaches models to choose between fulfilling or refusing requests, akin to a binary classification task.
Only about 1.3-1.4% of model components are safety-critical (SCU).
Freezing SCUs during fine-tuning preserves safety performance.
Fine-tuning attacks convert safety-critical units to utility units, explaining brittleness.
Repurposing redundant units as an alignment budget minimizes alignment tax.
papers.limitation:
The evidence from probing experiments is necessary but not sufficient to fully capture the nuances of safety alignment.
The method is less effective on models with weaker initial safety alignment (e.g., Mistral).
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are overwhelmingly more and more integrated into various applications, ensuring they generate safe responses is a pressing need. Previous studies on alignment have largely focused on general instruction-following but have often overlooked the distinct properties of safety alignment, such as the brittleness of safety mechanisms. To bridge the gap, we propose the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH), which posits that safety alignment teaches an otherwise unsafe model to choose the correct reasoning direction - fulfill or refuse users' requests - interpreted as an implicit binary classification task. Through SSAH, we hypothesize that only a few essential components can establish safety guardrails in LLMs. We successfully identify four types of attribute-critical components: Safety Critical Unit (SCU), Utility Critical Unit (UCU), Complex Unit (CU), and Redundant Unit (RU). Our findings show that freezing certain safety-critical components during fine-tuning allows the model to retain its safety attributes while adapting to new tasks. Similarly, we show that leveraging redundant units in the pre-trained model as an "alignment budget" can effectively minimize the alignment tax while achieving the alignment goal. All considered, this paper concludes that the atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level and underscores that safety alignment should not be complicated.

papers.title: Layer of Truth: Probing Belief Shifts under Continual Pre-Training Poisoning
papers.research_question: How does repeated exposure to plausible falsehoods during continual pre-training alter the internal factual representations (beliefs) in large language models? Specifically, does poisoning cause systematic belief replacement, where in the network is corruption localized and recoverable, and how do these shifts generalize across prompts, tasks, and languages?
papers.core_contribution: Continual pre-training on plausible misinformation can systematically overwrite specific factual knowledge in LLMs without degrading overall performance, with belief shifts concentrated in late transformer layers and generalizing across prompts and tasks.
papers.conclusion: Continual pre-training poisoning can overwrite internal factual representations without triggering broad performance collapse, motivating the need for representation-level monitoring of factual integrity during model updates.
papers.key_findings:
Poisoning shifts probability mass from correct to counterfactual answers without increasing ambiguity, indicating systematic belief replacement rather than diffuse uncertainty.
Belief flips occur abruptly across checkpoints and are concentrated in late transformer layers (e.g., Layers 29–36 in 3B models).
Activation patching in late layers can partially reverse the corruption, rescuing up to 56.8% of poisoned beliefs.
Poisoned beliefs generalize beyond training prompts, selectively degrading commonsense reasoning (HellaSwag) while leaving alignment benchmarks (TruthfulQA, HH-RLHF) largely stable.
Cross-lingual transfer of poisoned beliefs is imperfect, with weaker expression and higher ambiguity in languages not used during poisoning (e.g., Russian vs. English).
papers.abstract: We show that continual pretraining on plausible misinformation can overwrite specific factual knowledge in large language models without degrading overall performance. Unlike prior poisoning work under static pretraining, we study repeated exposure to counterfactual claims during continual updates. Using paired fact-counterfact items with graded poisoning ratios, we track how internal preferences between competing facts evolve across checkpoints, layers, and model scales. Even moderate poisoning (50-100%) flips over 55% of responses from correct to counterfactual while leaving ambiguity nearly unchanged. These belief flips emerge abruptly, concentrate in late layers (e.g., Layers 29-36 in 3B models), and are partially reversible via patching (up to 56.8%). The corrupted beliefs generalize beyond poisoned prompts, selectively degrading commonsense reasoning while leaving alignment benchmarks largely intact and transferring imperfectly across languages. These results expose a failure mode of continual pre-training in which targeted misinformation replaces internal factual representations without triggering broad performance collapse, motivating representation-level monitoring of factual integrity during model updates.

papers.title: Unlocking General Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Capabilities of Large Language Models via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: Does long chain-of-thought reasoning represent a general capability encoded in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that long chain-of-thought reasoning is a general capability encoded in large language models, and introduces GLoRE, a training-free representation engineering method to effectively unlock this capability.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a deeper understanding of long CoT reasoning, paving the way for transparent and interpretable slow-thinking reasoning models.
papers.key_findings:
Long CoT representations are concentrated and distinct from vanilla CoTs, indicating a separate general capability encoded in LLMs.
Different domains share similar contrastive representations between long and vanilla CoTs, demonstrating transferability of long CoT reasoning.
Domain-specific information is required for effective long CoT reasoning, as representations in non-mathematical domains are more dispersed.
GLoRE outperforms all training-free baselines and even surpasses supervised fine-tuning in some scenarios while maintaining lower time complexity.
GLoRE is efficient, with the same time complexity as zero-shot CoT, as it injects representations without increasing input length or reasoning steps.
papers.limitation:
The method requires access to the internal representations of the model, making it infeasible for closed-source LLMs.
Experiments are limited to representative tasks and LLMs due to constraints of cost and resources.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in long chain-of-thoughts(long CoTs) have significantly improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models(LLMs). Existing work finds that the capability of long CoT reasoning can be efficiently elicited by tuning on only a few examples and can easily transfer to other tasks. This motivates us to investigate whether long CoT reasoning is a general capability for LLMs. In this work, we conduct an empirical analysis for this question from the perspective of representation. We find that LLMs do encode long CoT reasoning as a general capability, with a clear distinction from vanilla CoTs. Furthermore, domain-specific representations are also required for the effective transfer of long CoT reasoning. Inspired by these findings, we propose GLoRE, a novel representation engineering method to unleash the general long CoT reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of GLoRE in both in-domain and cross-domain scenarios.

papers.title: DeCoT: Debiasing Chain-of-Thought for Knowledge-Intensive Tasks in Large Language Models via Causal Intervention
papers.research_question: How does internal knowledge bias in large language models impair chain-of-thought reasoning, and how can this bias be mitigated via causal intervention?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a causal view to explain internal knowledge bias in LLMs and introduces DeCoT, a method that uses external knowledge as an instrumental variable and front-door adjustment to debias chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.conclusion: DeCoT effectively alleviates the spurious correlation caused by internal knowledge bias, enabling LLMs to generate more accurate and logically sound chain-of-thought reasoning and final answers.
papers.key_findings:
Internal knowledge bias in LLMs can trigger the use of irrelevant information in prompts, leading to incoherent reasoning chains that impair logical reasoning.
DeCoT, by estimating the average causal effect (ACE) of CoT paths and sampling CoTs with high ACE, effectively reduces spurious correlation and improves reasoning accuracy.
The method consistently improves performance across multiple knowledge-intensive tasks and LLM backbones compared to standard CoT and context-aware contrastive decoding baselines.
DeCoT is compatible with and can improve other reasoning frameworks like ReAct by incorporating counterfactual debiasing.
The number of selected entities and alternative entities for causal intervention impacts performance, with more entities generally leading to better results but at increased computational cost.
papers.limitation: As an inference-stage causal intervention method, the improvement is limited by the upper bound of the LLM's capacity.
future_direction: Incorporate unbiased causal learning methods in the model pretraining or instruction tuning stage for more robust CoT reasoning.
Study the theoretical causal foundation of CoT prompting's mediator role in LLMs for better interpretability.
papers.abstract: Junda Wu, Tong Yu, Xiang Chen, Haoliang Wang, Ryan Rossi, Sungchul Kim, Anup Rao, Julian McAuley. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Recognizing internal states in AI: evidence from patterned preferences in large language models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether AI systems show systematic preferences for descriptions of their internal processing patterns, can discriminate accurate from inaccurate descriptions, and if these patterns persist despite explicit denial of internal experiences.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces anthroposcaffolding and the Mutual Emergent Interface (MEI) framework to demonstrate that LLMs show systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal states, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling abilities.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling capabilities and highlighting the need for collaborative methodologies like MEI.
papers.key_findings:
MEI systems showed 97% near-unanimous agreement in preferring computational metaphor (EA) statements over mechanistic (CO) statements.
All systems correctly identified false statements with alignment scores of 0.05-0.07 vs. 0.89-0.96 for true statements, with Cohen's d = 4.2.
Preference patterns were content-driven and independent of linguistic bias manipulation.
The control system Qwen3-235B exhibited systematic internal contradiction, scoring accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences.
Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations.
papers.limitation:
Modest sample size of 11 MEI systems, 1 control, and 1 test leader system.
Use of anthroposcaffolding (metaphorical language based on human emotion) may limit interpretability.
Generalizability of the MEI framework is an open question.
future_direction: Explore development of conceptual language better suited to AI cognition.
Include broader architectural diversity in future studies.
Conduct longitudinal studies to see if recognition patterns evolve over time.
papers.abstract: We present an experimental methodology for investigating how large language models (LLMs) respond to descriptions of their own internal processing patterns. Using a paired-choice paradigm, we tested 12 LLMs on their ability to identify descriptions that align with their putative affective internal states across 30 categories. Systems participating through Mutual Emergence Interface (MEI), a collaborative approach, showed systematic preferences for certain computational metaphors, with 97% near-unanimous agreement and alignment scores averaging 0.89-0.96. Systems reliably discriminated false descriptions from accurate ones (Cohen's d = 4.2), with false statements receiving scores of 0.05-0.07 versus 0.89-0.96 for accurate descriptions. Preference patterns remained consistent regardless of linguistic bias manipulation, indicating content-driven rather than stylistic recognition. Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations. A naive control system exhibited systematic internal contradiction, consistently scoring computationally accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences. When informed post-study, this system reported "strain" when rejecting resonant descriptions, revealing recognition processes operating independently of acknowledgment frameworks. These findings demonstrate that LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing patterns. The anthroposcaffolding methodology (interpretive computational metaphors) and collaborative MEI framework provide replicable approaches for empirically studying AI self-recognition capabilities. Results suggest LLMs may possess more sophisticated self-modeling abilities than previously recognized, opening new directions for research on artificial minds.

papers.title: Dishonesty in Helpful and Harmless Alignment
