papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally encode representations of reasoning correctness, with strongest signals in middle-late layers, and they distinguish between logical and semantic equivalence in abstract reasoning concepts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess internal representations of reasoning correctness and abstraction, which can inform future efforts to enhance model reliability, interpretability, and trustworthiness.
papers.key_findings:
A classifier trained on LLM activations achieves over 80% accuracy in predicting reasoning step correctness.
LLMs have internal representations of reasoning correctness, strongest in middle-late Transformer layers.
LLMs encode abstract reasoning concepts that separate logical from semantic equivalence.
Abstraction level varies across layers, with middle layers containing more abstract information.
The reasoning representations are similar across top-performing layers, suggesting redundant encoding.
papers.limitation:
Analysis restricted to structured logic puzzles, may not generalize to real-world scenarios.
Classifier's success may not generalize to other types of reasoning problems.
Reliance on probing techniques does not provide mechanistic explanation of how representations emerge.
Classifier trained on single LLM architecture, generalizability across models unclear.
future_direction: Explore more diverse reasoning benchmarks.
Conduct broader cross-model analyses including LRM models.
Develop methods for directly steering LLM reasoning based on learned representations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive capabilities but struggle with reasoning errors due to hallucinations and flawed logic. To investigate their internal representations of reasoning, we introduce ArrangementPuzzle, a novel puzzle dataset with structured solutions and automated stepwise correctness verification. We trained a classifier model on LLM activations on this dataset and found that it achieved over 80% accuracy in predicting reasoning correctness, implying that LLMs internally distinguish between correct and incorrect reasoning steps, with the strongest representations in middle-late Transformer layers. Further analysis reveals that LLMs encode abstract reasoning concepts within the middle activation layers of the transformer architecture, distinguishing logical from semantic equivalence. These findings provide insights into LLM reasoning mechanisms and contribute to improving AI reliability and interpretability, thereby offering the possibility to manipulate and refine LLM reasoning.

papers.title: HeadHunt-VAD: Hunting Robust Anomaly-Sensitive Heads in MLLM for Tuning-Free Video Anomaly Detection
papers.research_question: How can we perform video anomaly detection without fine-tuning by directly identifying and leveraging a sparse set of robust, anomaly-sensitive attention heads within a frozen Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM)?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a tuning-free video anomaly detection paradigm that identifies a sparse set of robust, anomaly-sensitive attention heads within a frozen MLLM and uses their features for efficient and accurate detection.
papers.conclusion: HeadHunt-V AD validates head-level probing in frozen MLLMs as a powerful and practical paradigm for real-world video anomaly detection, achieving superior performance with remarkable computational and data efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
HeadHunt-V AD achieves state-of-the-art performance among tuning-free methods on UCF-Crime (87.03% AUC) and XD-Violence (82.63% AP).
The Robust Head Identification (RHI) module effectively identifies heads that are discriminative and stable across diverse prompts.
The method is highly efficient, requiring only a single forward pass, minimal data (1% of training set), and low feature dimensionality.
Features from the selected expert heads form well-separated clusters in the feature space, confirming their discriminative power.
The lightweight logistic regression anomaly scorer and calibrated temporal locator enable accurate detection and localization with high interpretability.
papers.abstract: Video Anomaly Detection (VAD) aims to locate events that deviate from normal patterns in videos. Traditional approaches often rely on extensive labeled data and incur high computational costs. Recent tuning-free methods based on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a promising alternative by leveraging their rich world knowledge. However, these methods typically rely on textual outputs, which introduces information loss, exhibits normalcy bias, and suffers from prompt sensitivity, making them insufficient for capturing subtle anomalous cues. To address these constraints, we propose HeadHunt-VAD, a novel tuning-free VAD paradigm that bypasses textual generation by directly hunting robust anomaly-sensitive internal attention heads within the frozen MLLM. Central to our method is a Robust Head Identification module that systematically evaluates all attention heads using a multi-criteria analysis of saliency and stability, identifying a sparse subset of heads that are consistently discriminative across diverse prompts. Features from these expert heads are then fed into a lightweight anomaly scorer and a temporal locator, enabling efficient and accurate anomaly detection with interpretable outputs. Extensive experiments show that HeadHunt-VAD achieves state-of-the-art performance among tuning-free methods on two major VAD benchmarks while maintaining high efficiency, validating head-level probing in MLLMs as a powerful and practical solution for real-world anomaly detection.

papers.title: Hallucination Detection via Internal States and Structured Reasoning Consistency in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the Detection Dilemma in hallucination detection, and how can it be resolved by unifying internal state probing and chain-of-thought verification?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a unified framework for hallucination detection that combines internal state probing and chain-of-thought verification, overcoming the Detection Dilemma through multi-path signal generation and cross-attention fusion.
papers.conclusion: The unified framework effectively resolves the Detection Dilemma by bridging sub-symbolic and symbolic signals, demonstrating robust hallucination detection across diverse tasks and representing a step towards trustworthy LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
The framework achieves state-of-the-art AUROC scores on TruthfulQA, TriviaQA, and GSM8K, outperforming both ISP and CoTV baselines.
Ablation studies reveal that all three signal paths (internal states, CoT, reverse inference) contribute non-linearly to performance, indicating deep integration.
Optimal detection uses representations from late layers (e.g., 24th) and text generated at higher temperature (T=0.8).
Unified representations provide better discriminative power, as shown by t-SNE projections separating hallucination and non-hallucination samples.
Cross-attention weights highlight semantic contradictions between answers and reasoning traces, enhancing interpretability.
papers.abstract: The detection of sophisticated hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) is hampered by a ``Detection Dilemma'': methods probing internal states (Internal State Probing) excel at identifying factual inconsistencies but fail on logical fallacies, while those verifying externalized reasoning (Chain-of-Thought Verification) show the opposite behavior. This schism creates a task-dependent blind spot: Chain-of-Thought Verification fails on fact-intensive tasks like open-domain QA where reasoning is ungrounded, while Internal State Probing is ineffective on logic-intensive tasks like mathematical reasoning where models are confidently wrong. We resolve this with a unified framework that bridges this critical gap. However, unification is hindered by two fundamental challenges: the Signal Scarcity Barrier, as coarse symbolic reasoning chains lack signals directly comparable to fine-grained internal states, and the Representational Alignment Barrier, a deep-seated mismatch between their underlying semantic spaces. To overcome these, we introduce a multi-path reasoning mechanism to obtain more comparable, fine-grained signals, and a segment-aware temporalized cross-attention module to adaptively fuse these now-aligned representations, pinpointing subtle dissonances. Extensive experiments on three diverse benchmarks and two leading LLMs demonstrate that our framework consistently and significantly outperforms strong baselines. Our code is available: https://github.com/peach918/HalluDet.

papers.title: Focus on Your Question! Interpreting and Mitigating Toxic CoT Problems in Commonsense Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism behind the Toxic CoT problem where Chain-of-Thought reasoning causes originally correct answers to turn wrong, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies the Toxic CoT problem, interprets it as information loss from the question in shallow attention layers during CoT reasoning, and proposes RIDERS to mitigate the problem by compensating for the information deficit.
papers.conclusion: RIDERS effectively mitigates the Toxic CoT problem and improves the model's commonsense reasoning performance.
papers.key_findings:
Toxic CoT accounts for 37% of CoT errors in white-box models and 33% in black-box models on average.
Rationale Drift and Answer Drift are caused by information loss from the question in shallow attention layers.
The proposed RIDERS method reduces the proportion of Toxic CoT by 23.6% and improves overall accuracy by 5.5%.
future_direction: Extend the method to more complex reasoning tasks.
Explore applicability in other domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit high-level commonsense reasoning abilities, especially with enhancement methods like Chain-of-Thought (CoT). However, we find these CoT-like methods lead to a considerable number of originally correct answers turning wrong, which we define as the Toxic CoT problem. To interpret and mitigate this problem, we first utilize attribution tracing and causal tracing methods to probe the internal working mechanism of the LLM during CoT reasoning. Through comparisons, we prove that the model exhibits information loss from the question over the shallow attention layers when generating rationales or answers. Based on the probing findings, we design a novel method called RIDERS (Residual decodIng and sERial-position Swap), which compensates for the information deficit in the model from both decoding and serial-position perspectives. Through extensive experiments on multiple commonsense reasoning benchmarks, we validate that this method not only significantly eliminates Toxic CoT problems (decreased by 23.6%), but also effectively improves the model's overall commonsense reasoning performance (increased by 5.5%).

papers.title: Refusal Falls off a Cliff: How Safety Alignment Fails in Reasoning?
papers.research_question: What mechanism makes the safety alignment vulnerable in reasoning models?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies the 'refusal cliff' failure mode in reasoning models, causally links it to a sparse set of 'Refusal Suppression Heads', and introduces a data selection method (Cliff-as-a-Judge) that efficiently repairs safety alignment using minimal data.
papers.conclusion: The work identifies and mechanistically characterizes the refusal cliff safety failure, links it to specific attention heads, and proposes an efficient data selection method for safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Many poorly-aligned reasoning models correctly identify harmful prompts and maintain strong refusal intentions during thinking, but experience a sharp drop (refusal cliff) at the final tokens before output generation.
A sparse set of attention heads (Refusal Suppression Heads) causally contribute to the refusal cliff by suppressing refusal-related representations.
Ablating just 3% of these heads can reduce attack success rates below 10%.
The proposed Cliff-as-a-Judge data selection method, which selects examples with the largest refusal cliff, achieves comparable safety improvements using only 1.7% of the vanilla safety training data.
The refusal cliff is localized to final tokens, amplified in deeper layers, preceded by a plateau, and depends on the model's thinking process.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic analysis focuses primarily on attention heads, leaving other architectural components such as MLP blocks, positional encodings, and cross-layer interactions underexplored.
The data selection method depends on having access to the model's internal representations and refusal scores, which may be impractical for proprietary systems.
future_direction: Investigation of proxy metrics or black-box analogues for the data selection method.
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) with multi-step reasoning capabilities have shown remarkable problem-solving abilities, yet they exhibit concerning safety vulnerabilities that remain poorly understood. In this work, we investigate why safety alignment fails in reasoning models through a mechanistic interpretability lens. Using a linear probing approach to trace refusal intentions across token positions, we discover a striking phenomenon termed as \textbf{refusal cliff}: many poorly-aligned reasoning models correctly identify harmful prompts and maintain strong refusal intentions during their thinking process, but experience a sharp drop in refusal scores at the final tokens before output generation. This suggests that these models are not inherently unsafe; rather, their refusal intentions are systematically suppressed. Through causal intervention analysis, we identify a sparse set of attention heads that negatively contribute to refusal behavior. Ablating just 3\% of these heads can reduce attack success rates below 10\%. Building on these mechanistic insights, we propose \textbf{Cliff-as-a-Judge}, a novel data selection method that identifies training examples exhibiting the largest refusal cliff to efficiently repair reasoning models' safety alignment. This approach achieves comparable safety improvements using only 1.7\% of the vanilla safety training data, demonstrating a less-is-more effect in safety alignment.

papers.title: Behind the Scene: Revealing the Secrets of Pre-trained Vision-and-Language Models
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained vision-and-language models work internally? Specifically, the paper investigates multimodal fusion, modality importance, cross-modal interaction, visual relations, and linguistic knowledge in these models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces VALUE, a set of probing tasks for vision-and-language models, and uses it to analyze UNITER and LXMERT, revealing that textual modality is more dominant, a subset of heads specialize in cross-modal interaction, and visual relations and linguistic knowledge are encoded.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into the inner workings of pre-trained V+L models and offers guidelines for future model design, such as preferring single-stream architecture and initializing with BERT weights.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models attend more to text than images during inference.
A subset of attention heads are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions.
Learned attention matrices show patterns coherent with latent alignment between image regions and textual words.
Attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions.
Linguistic knowledge is effectively encoded in the attention heads.
future_direction: Perform model compression via pruning attention heads based on the analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent Transformer-based large-scale pre-trained models have revolutionized vision-and-language (V+L) research. Models such as ViLBERT, LXMERT and UNITER have significantly lifted state of the art across a wide range of V+L benchmarks with joint image-text pre-training. However, little is known about the inner mechanisms that destine their impressive success. To reveal the secrets behind the scene of these powerful models, we present VALUE (Vision-And-Language Understanding Evaluation), a set of meticulously designed probing tasks (e.g., Visual Coreference Resolution, Visual Relation Detection, Linguistic Probing Tasks) generalizable to standard pre-trained V+L models, aiming to decipher the inner workings of multimodal pre-training (e.g., the implicit knowledge garnered in individual attention heads, the inherent cross-modal alignment learned through contextualized multimodal embeddings). Through extensive analysis of each archetypal model architecture via these probing tasks, our key observations are: (i) Pre-trained models exhibit a propensity for attending over text rather than images during inference. (ii) There exists a subset of attention heads that are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions. (iii) Learned attention matrix in pre-trained models demonstrates patterns coherent with the latent alignment between image regions and textual words. (iv) Plotted attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions. (v) Pure linguistic knowledge is also effectively encoded in the attention heads. These are valuable insights serving to guide future work towards designing better model architecture and objectives for multimodal pre-training.

papers.title: What Makes Chain-of-Thought Prompting Effective? A Counterfactual Study
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms behind the effectiveness of Chain-of-Thought prompting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that the effectiveness of Chain-of-Thought prompting stems from its ability to convey task understanding through consistent patterns and web-style text, rather than the specific symbols used. It also shows that COT helps models fill in missing commonsense information, especially for difficult reasoning problems and long-tail questions.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that Chain-of-Thought prompting works by efficiently communicating task understanding and leveraging the model's ability to fill in commonsense knowledge, rather than by teaching step-by-step reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Specific symbols in the prompt do not significantly impact performance, but consistent patterns and web-style text are crucial.
The necessity of accurate few-shot examples depends on their role in communicating task understanding; inaccurate examples can sometimes improve performance.
Intermediate steps in COT primarily convey task understanding rather than teaching how to solve the task.
COT leverages LLMs to fill in missing commonsense information, aiding difficult reasoning and long-tail questions.
Patterns and symbols work together to generate missing information and reinforce task understanding.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to a few tasks and models.
The definitions of symbols and patterns are task-specific and may not generalize.
Reliance on automatic metrics may not capture nuanced errors.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to more tasks and models.
Incorporate human evaluation.
Explore generalization of symbols and patterns definitions.
papers.abstract: The effectiveness of Chain-of-thought prompting (CoT) has been widely recognized, but the underlying mechanisms behind its success, the reason why it just works for a wide range of tasks, remains an open question. To investigate this, we employ a counterfactual prompting approach, systematically manipulating elements of examples used in a few-shot prompt, and testing the consequences on model behavior. This allows us to understand the relative contributions of prompt elements such as symbols (digits, entities) and patterns (equations, sentence structure) on in-context learning. Our experiments with three different large language models (LLMs) reveal several key findings. First, the specific symbols used in the prompt do not significantly impact the model’s performance. However, consistent patterns in examples and specifying text in style frequently found on the web are crucial. Second, our findings suggest that the necessity of accurate few-shot examples depends on their role in communicating task understanding. We identify tasks where inaccurate few-shot examples hurt and, surprisingly, tasks where they improve performance. Additionally, we find that the intermediate steps in CoT may not necessarily facilitate learning how to solve a task, but instead efficiently convey task understanding (what) to the model. Furthermore, CoT leverages LLMs to fill in missing commonsense information, particularly helping difficult reasoning problems and long-tail questions.

papers.title: What Makes a Good Reasoning Chain? Uncovering Structural Patterns in Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: What structural patterns in long chain-of-thought reasoning drive or predict the correctness of final answers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LCoT2Tree, an automated framework for converting long chain-of-thought reasoning into hierarchical tree structures, enabling structural analysis that predicts reasoning success and reveals error patterns.
papers.conclusion: LCoT2Tree is a powerful tool for diagnosing, interpreting, and improving reasoning in LLMs, highlighting the critical role of structural analysis in understanding reasoning chains.
papers.key_findings:
Structural patterns extracted by LCoT2Tree are stronger predictors of reasoning success than length-based features across diverse tasks and models.
Error patterns such as over-branching, step redundancy, direct reasoning, and skipped thinking are identified in incorrect reasoning chains.
Reasoning behaviors vary across tasks, with different structural patterns for math, code, and science tasks.
Different models exhibit distinguishable reasoning styles on the same task, as captured by LCoT2Tree.
LCoT2Tree improves Best-of-N decoding by selecting well-structured reasoning chains, enhancing accuracy in complex tasks.
papers.limitation:
Structural analysis alone cannot capture semantic errors or recognize correct reasoning that deviates from common structural patterns.
As models improve and produce more coherent reasoning by default, the value of structural diagnostics may decrease.
LCoT2Tree is computationally expensive due to reliance on off-the-shelf large language models for tree construction.
future_direction: Integrate semantic reasoning signals with structural analysis to achieve a more holistic understanding of LLM reasoning behaviors.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in reasoning with large language models (LLMs) have popularized Long Chain-of-Thought (LCoT), a strategy that encourages deliberate and step-by-step reasoning before producing a final answer. While LCoTs have enabled expert-level performance in complex tasks, how the internal structures of their reasoning chains drive, or even predict, the correctness of final answers remains a critical yet underexplored question. In this work, we present LCoT2Tree, an automated framework that converts sequential LCoTs into hierarchical tree structures and thus enables deeper structural analysis of LLM reasoning. Using graph neural networks (GNNs), we reveal that structural patterns extracted by LCoT2Tree, including exploration, backtracking, and verification, serve as stronger predictors of final performance across a wide range of tasks and models. Leveraging an explainability technique, we further identify critical thought patterns such as over-branching that account for failures. Beyond diagnostic insights, the structural patterns by LCoT2Tree support practical applications, including improving Best-of-N decoding effectiveness. Overall, our results underscore the critical role of internal structures of reasoning chains, positioning LCoT2Tree as a powerful tool for diagnosing, interpreting, and improving reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Identify Reasoning Features in Language Models?
papers.research_question: How reliably do sparse autoencoder (SAE) features, identified via contrastive methods, capture genuine reasoning processes in language models, as opposed to superficial lexical or stylistic correlates?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoder features identified as 'reasoning features' via contrastive methods are often superficial, triggered by lexical cues or stylistic patterns that co-occur with reasoning, rather than capturing the underlying reasoning process itself.
papers.conclusion: Sparse decompositions can favor low-dimensional correlates that co-occur with reasoning, underscoring the need for falsification when attributing high-level behaviors to individual SAE features.
papers.key_findings:
45–90% of contrastively selected SAE 'reasoning features' are triggered by injecting just a few associated tokens into non-reasoning text.
For remaining context-dependent features, LLM-guided falsification generates non-reasoning false positives and meaning-preserving paraphrases of reasoning traces that suppress activation, decoupling activation from reasoning behavior.
Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers, and reasoning datasets, no features were found that robustly satisfied the criteria for genuine reasoning behavior.
A theoretical analysis shows sparsity in SAE decoding can bias features towards stable low-dimensional correlates (e.g., lexical cues) over high-dimensional within-behavior variation.
Steering candidate features yielded minimal or slightly degraded performance on reasoning benchmarks, indicating activation changes do not imply representation of reasoning computations.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to the specific models, SAEs, and reasoning datasets analyzed; genuine reasoning features might exist in other settings or require different detection methods.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying genuine reasoning features that are robust to superficial confounds.
Exploring whether genuine reasoning is represented in a more distributed manner across many features rather than in individual SAE features.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether sparse autoencoders identify genuine reasoning features in large language models. We first present a stylized theoretical analysis showing that sparsity-regularized decoding favors stable low-dimensional correlates over high-dimensional within-reasoning variation, biasing learned features toward token-level cues. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce a falsification-based evaluation framework that combines causal token injection with LLM-guided counterexample generation to distinguish genuine reasoning features from superficial linguistic correlates. Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers and datasets, we find that contrastively selected reasoning features are highly sensitive to token interventions, with 45%-90% activating when only a few associated tokens are injected into non-reasoning text. For the remaining features, LLM-guided falsification reliably constructs non-reasoning inputs that instantiate the feature's token-level cues and trigger activation, and meaning-preserving paraphrases of top-activating reasoning traces that suppress it. Steering the highest-ranked features yields no improvements on benchmarks. Overall, our results suggest that when low-dimensional token-level patterns are coupled with high-dimensional reasoning processes, the sparsity bias of SAEs systematically favors low-dimensional linguistic patterns that consistently co-occur with reasoning. Code is available at https://github.com/GeorgeMLP/reasoning-probing.

papers.title: Exploration and adaptation of large language models for specialized domains
papers.research_question: Can large language models overcome challenges in specialized domains, and how can they be effectively adapted to domain-specific requirements?
papers.core_contribution: The dissertation provides insights into the inner workings of LLMs and proposes adaptation methods that demonstrate LLMs can be effectively used in specialized domains, particularly clinical NLP.
papers.conclusion: The work provides new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models and multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.
papers.key_findings:
Layers of Transformer-based LLMs encode different dimensions of input text, with contextual representations and general language knowledge being beneficial for complex tasks.
Pre-trained language models outperform traditional approaches on clinical tasks.
Integration of domain-specific resources (like ICD hierarchy) improves model generalization.
Behavioral testing framework can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts.
Prototypical networks can provide interpretable diagnosis predictions.
papers.limitation: There is no ground truth in clinical data
future_direction: Integration of multimodal and multilingual data
Efficient methods for large language models
papers.abstract: Large language models have transformed the field of natural language processing (NLP). Their improved performance on various NLP benchmarks makes them a promising tool—also for the application in specialized domains. Such domains are characterized by highly trained professionals with particular domain expertise. Since these experts are rare, improving the efficiency of their work with automated systems is especially desirable. However, domain-specific text resources hold various challenges for NLP systems. These challenges include distinct language, noisy and scarce data, and a high level of variation. Further, specialized domains present an increased need for transparent systems since they are often applied in high stakes settings. In this dissertation, we examine whether large language models (LLMs) can overcome some of these challenges and propose methods to effectively adapt them to domain-specific requirements. We first investigate the inner workings and abilities of LLMs and show how they can fill the gaps that are present in previous NLP algorithms for specialized domains. To this end, we explore the sources of errors produced by earlier systems to identify which of them can be addressed by using LLMs. Following this, we take a closer look at how information is processed within Transformer-based LLMs to better understand their capabilities. We find that their layers encode different dimensions of the input text. Here, the contextual vector representation, and the general language knowledge learned during pre-training are especially beneficial for solving complex and multi-step tasks common in specialized domains. Following this exploration, we propose solutions for further adapting LLMs to the requirements of domain-specific tasks. We focus on the clinical domain, which incorporates many typical challenges found in specialized domains. We show how to improve generalization by integrating different domain-specific resources into our models. We further analyze the behavior of the produced models and propose a behavioral testing framework that can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts. Finally, we present an approach for incorporating the benefits of LLMs while fulfilling requirements such as interpretability and modularity. The presented solutions show improvements in performance on benchmark datasets and in manually conducted analyses with medical professionals. Our work provides both new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models as well as multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.

papers.title: Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior
papers.research_question: Can the internal representations of language models predict their eventual behavior before any output token is generated?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on the internal representations of input tokens can predict a wide range of eventual behaviors of language models, and when combined with conformal prediction, provide provable bounds on estimation error for precise early warning systems.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of language models contain information about eventual behavior, and conformal probes can provide reliable early warning systems for various behaviors, enabling efficient and safe deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on hidden states of input tokens can predict instruction-following failures with high consistency, outperforming a fine-tuned BERT baseline.
Conformal probes can detect safety alignment failures (jailbreaking) and reduce jailbreak success rate from 30% to 2.7%, a 91% reduction.
Probes can preemptively estimate an LM's confidence as measured by per-token perplexity, a behavior that cannot be inferred from output text alone.
When applied to CoT prompting for text classification, conformal probes reduce inference costs by 65% on average across 27 datasets with negligible accuracy loss.
Probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting favorable scaling properties.
papers.limitation:
The approach relies on the exchangeability assumption for conformal prediction, which may not hold in practice.
The method was only tested on a few datasets and with a few runs.
papers.abstract: The text produced by language models (LMs) can exhibit specific `behaviors,' such as a failure to follow alignment training, that we hope to detect and react to during deployment. Identifying these behaviors can often only be done post facto, i.e., after the entire text of the output has been generated. We provide evidence that there are times when we can predict how an LM will behave early in computation, before even a single token is generated. We show that probes trained on the internal representation of input tokens alone can predict a wide range of eventual behaviors over the entire output sequence. Using methods from conformal prediction, we provide provable bounds on the estimation error of our probes, creating precise early warning systems for these behaviors. The conformal probes can identify instances that will trigger alignment failures (jailbreaking) and instruction-following failures, without requiring a single token to be generated. An early warning system built on the probes reduces jailbreaking by 91%. Our probes also show promise in pre-emptively estimating how confident the model will be in its response, a behavior that cannot be detected using the output text alone. Conformal probes can preemptively estimate the final prediction of an LM that uses Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, hence accelerating inference. When applied to an LM that uses CoT to perform text classification, the probes drastically reduce inference costs (65% on average across 27 datasets), with negligible accuracy loss. Encouragingly, probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting applicability to the largest of models in real-world settings.

papers.title: Exploring the Hidden Reasoning Process of Large Language Models by Misleading Them
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) truly engage in task abstraction and rule-based reasoning beyond mere memorization?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Misleading Fine-Tuning (MisFT), an evaluation paradigm free from data contamination, and finds that LLMs can generalize contradictory rules to novel domains, suggesting an internal abstraction-reasoning mechanism.
papers.conclusion: MisFT provides evidence that LLMs possess human-like reasoning abilities through abstraction and rule-based reasoning, and it can serve as a tool for assessing generalization in various tasks and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can learn contradictory arithmetic rules through fine-tuning and apply them to solve math word problems, showing out-of-distribution generalization.
Larger models exhibit better generalization performance, indicating a positive correlation between model size and reasoning ability.
LLMs can generalize overloaded logical rules from formulas to natural language reasoning tasks in first-order logic.
Vision-language models (VLMs) can generalize contradictory rules learned from text to image-based arithmetic problems without seeing images during fine-tuning.
Deep layers in LLMs are crucial for abstraction and reasoning, as freezing them sharply reduces generalization accuracy on math word problems.
papers.limitation:
The paper does not pinpoint the actual circuits for abstraction and reasoning in the model's computational graph, leaving it for future work.
MisFT may cause catastrophic forgetting and is a disruptive probing method that could harm the model's general reasoning ability.
future_direction: Accurately pinpointing the circuits for abstraction and reasoning using more advanced mechanistic interpretation methods.
Applying MisFT to assess reasoning and generalization capabilities in a wider range of tasks and modalities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been able to perform various forms of reasoning tasks in a wide range of scenarios, but are they truly engaging in task abstraction and rule-based reasoning beyond mere memorization? To answer this question, we propose a novel experimental approach, Misleading Fine-Tuning (MisFT), to examine whether LLMs perform abstract reasoning by altering their original understanding of fundamental rules. In particular, by constructing datasets with math expressions or logical formulas that contradict correct principles, we fine-tune the model to learn those contradictory rules and assess its generalization ability on unseen test domains. Through a series of experiments, we find that current LLMs are capable of applying contradictory rules to solve practical math word problems and natural language reasoning tasks, implying the presence of an internal mechanism in LLMs that abstracts before reasoning.

papers.title: Thinking About Thinking: SAGE-nano's Inverse Reasoning for Self-Aware Language Models
papers.research_question: How can large language models be enabled to introspect on and explain their own reasoning processes, specifically why they choose particular reasoning chains over alternatives?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces inverse reasoning, a paradigm enabling LLMs to introspect on their own reasoning processes via attention pathway reconstruction, and presents SAGE-nano, a 4B-parameter model that demonstrates this capability, improving both reasoning transparency and performance.
papers.conclusion: The inverse reasoning paradigm enables LLMs to introspect on their reasoning and generate interpretable explanations, enhancing transparency and trustworthiness while maintaining competitive performance, establishing foundations for transparent AI systems in safety, education, and scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
SAGE-nano achieves competitive reasoning accuracy (e.g., 74.6% on AQUA-RAT) and high explanation quality (92.1% human preference score).
Inverse reasoning enhances both reasoning transparency and forward reasoning performance, as shown by ablation studies.
The model demonstrates superior introspection accuracy in identifying decision points, alternative paths, and confidence calibration.
The architecture can be trained and deployed efficiently on consumer hardware (Mac Mini M1 cluster), making advanced reasoning more accessible.
Inverse reasoning addresses critical AI safety challenges by providing interpretable explanations of model decision-making.
papers.limitation:
The inverse reasoning approach adds significant computational overhead (40% inference time), limiting scalability to larger models.
Current metrics for explanation quality rely heavily on subjective human evaluation; developing automated evaluation metrics remains an open problem.
Inverse reasoning explanations lack objective ground truth, making validation difficult.
The 4-billion parameter constraint limits the model's capacity for complex reasoning tasks compared to larger state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Investigating inverse reasoning capabilities in larger model architectures (scalability studies).
Extending inverse reasoning to visual and multi-modal reasoning tasks.
Developing robust automated metrics for explanation quality assessment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities at solving complex reasoning tasks with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, but their decision-making processes remain somewhat blackbox. We introduce textbfinverse reasoning, a novel paradigm enabling LLMs to decompose and explain their own reasoning chains post-hoc. Our approach, used in SAGE-nano, a 4-billion-parameter reasoning model, employs a metacognitive structure that reflects back via attention processes to identify major decision points and generate explanations of reasoning choices. While typical CoT approaches are directed towards forward reasoning generation, inverse reasoning provides insight into why specific reasoning chains were selected over others. Through thorough testing of logical reasoning puzzles, math problems and ethical dilemmas from AQUA-RAT, CommonsenseQA, and customized benchmarks, we demonstrate that SAGE-nano is at the cutting edge both on reasoning accuracy (74.6% on AQUA-RAT) and explanation quality (92.1% human preference score) for its task, and offers performance almost on par with models like Claude-3.5 Sonnet or GPT-4o. Our contributions are: (i) the first rigorous framework for LLM self-reflection via inverse reasoning, (ii) a novel metalearning framework to reverse the attention flow, (iii) comprehensive evaluation frameworks for reasoning transparency, and (iv) evidence that increasing reasoning using inverse reasoning improves interpretability along with reasoning performance. Our work creates new avenues for transparent AI systems and closes significant gaps in AI safety, education, and scientific discovery.

papers.title: Are language models aware of the road not taken? Token-level uncertainty and hidden state dynamics
papers.research_question: Do language models represent the alternate paths they could take during generation? How do hidden activations correlate with token-level uncertainty and steering success?
papers.core_contribution: Hidden activations in language models correlate with token-level uncertainty and can be used to steer generation and predict future outcome distributions, indicating that models implicitly represent alternate reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: Hidden activations in language models reflect token-level uncertainty and can be used to estimate outcome distributions efficiently, offering a way to understand and control model decision-making.
papers.key_findings:
Steering success correlates with token-level uncertainty: models are most steerable when they are least certain about the final answer.
Hidden activations contain information about the model's future outcome distribution, as linear probes on the model's own activations predict outcome distribution better than probes on another model's embeddings.
The dynamics of steering success and outcome distribution are similar, with abrupt changes at the same token positions identified by change point detection.
The correlation between steering success and base outcome probability is moderate (R=0.57) and consistent across examples (average R=0.64).
Linear probes are most predictive in middle layers (layers 6-10) of the model.
papers.limitation:
The computational cost of Forking Paths Analysis is high, requiring millions of tokens to analyze a single base path completion.
Only a handful of examples from three datasets are analyzed due to computational constraints.
papers.abstract: When a language model generates text, the selection of individual tokens might lead it down very different reasoning paths, making uncertainty difficult to quantify. In this work, we consider whether reasoning language models represent the alternate paths that they could take during generation. To test this hypothesis, we use hidden activations to control and predict a language model's uncertainty during chain-of-thought reasoning. In our experiments, we find a clear correlation between how uncertain a model is at different tokens, and how easily the model can be steered by controlling its activations. This suggests that activation interventions are most effective when there are alternate paths available to the model -- in other words, when it has not yet committed to a particular final answer. We also find that hidden activations can predict a model's future outcome distribution, demonstrating that models implicitly represent the space of possible paths.

papers.title: From Imitation to Introspection: Probing Self-Consciousness in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models possess self-consciousness, defined as global availability of information (C1) and self-monitoring (C2).
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces functional definitions of self-consciousness for language models and conducts a four-stage experiment (quantification, representation, manipulation, acquisition) to probe self-consciousness. Findings indicate that models are in early stages of self-consciousness, with internal representations that can be acquired via fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Current models exhibit a nascent level of self-consciousness with substantial potential for future development.
Models internally represent each of the ten self-consciousness concepts with visible activations, which can be classified into four categories (camelback, flat, oscillatory, fallback).
Different models exhibit similar activation patterns when processing the same concept, likely due to shared decoder-only transformer architecture.
Larger models seem to exhibit greater robustness against manipulation attempts.
Fine-tuning appears to activate representations of self-consciousness in the deeper layers, which capture semantic information.
papers.limitation: The study of self-consciousness in language models is uncharted territory, and even human self-consciousness is not fully understood.
papers.abstract: Self-consciousness, the introspection of one's existence and thoughts, represents a high-level cognitive process. As language models advance at an unprecedented pace, a critical question arises: Are these models becoming self-conscious? Drawing upon insights from psychological and neural science, this work presents a practical definition of self-consciousness for language models and refines ten core concepts. Our work pioneers an investigation into self-consciousness in language models by, for the first time, leveraging causal structural games to establish the functional definitions of the ten core concepts. Based on our definitions, we conduct a comprehensive four-stage experiment: quantification (evaluation of ten leading models), representation (visualization of self-consciousness within the models), manipulation (modification of the models' representation), and acquisition (fine-tuning the models on core concepts). Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning. Our datasets and code are at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/SelfConsciousness.

papers.title: Opening the Black Box: A Survey on the Mechanisms of Multi-Step Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that enable multi-step reasoning in large language models, covering both implicit (latent) and explicit (e.g., Chain-of-Thought) reasoning paradigms?
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying multi-step reasoning in large language models, organizing existing research around seven interconnected research questions and highlighting future research directions.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes by highlighting five open research directions for future mechanistic understanding of multi-step reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit multi-hop reasoning in LLMs is an orchestrated, layered process with distinct modules specializing in different phases, but it is constrained by the fixed depth of transformers.
Implicit reasoning capability emerges via grokking, a phase transition from memorization to generalization, influenced by training data distribution, data scale, and optimization biases.
LLMs frequently bypass genuine multi-step reasoning by using shortcuts, such as direct input-output associations (factual shortcuts) or surface-level heuristics (structural shortcuts).
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting activates a 'reasoning mode' where models use generated tokens as external memory, breaking the depth limitation and enhancing computational expressiveness and generalization.
CoT does not equate to faithful explainability; it often functions as post-hoc rationalization due to a structural mismatch between the distributed, parallel computation of transformers and the sequential nature of explicit reasoning.
future_direction: Rigorous causal analysis in real-world settings
Bridging the faithfulness gap of explicit CoT reasoning
Mechanistic understanding of Latent CoT reasoning
White-box evaluation metrics for LLM reasoning
From mechanistic interpretation to model control
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to solve problems requiring multiple reasoning steps, yet the internal mechanisms enabling such capabilities remain elusive. Unlike existing surveys that primarily focus on engineering methods to enhance performance, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying LLM multi-step reasoning. We organize the survey around a conceptual framework comprising seven interconnected research questions, from how LLMs execute implicit multi-hop reasoning within hidden activations to how verbalized explicit reasoning remodels the internal computation. Finally, we highlight five research directions for future mechanistic studies.

papers.title: From Explicit CoT to Implicit CoT: Learning to Internalize CoT Step by Step
papers.research_question: Can language models be taught to internalize chain-of-thought reasoning steps, thereby simplifying the reasoning process while maintaining high performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Stepwise Internalization, a method to internalize chain-of-thought reasoning by gradually removing intermediate steps during training, enabling models to achieve high accuracy without explicit CoT generation.
papers.conclusion: Stepwise Internalization enables implicit CoT reasoning, achieving high accuracy and faster inference compared to explicit CoT, and demonstrates the potential of internalizing reasoning steps in language models.
papers.key_findings:
Stepwise Internalization enables a GPT-2 Small model to solve 9-by-9 multiplication with up to 99% accuracy, whereas standard training fails beyond 4-by-4 multiplication.
On GSM8K, Stepwise Internalization achieves over 50% accuracy with Mistral 7B without explicit CoT, outperforming GPT-4 without CoT (44%).
Stepwise Internalization lags behind explicit CoT in accuracy but is faster, achieving up to 11x speedup on 9x9 multiplication.
The method allows trading off accuracy and speed by internalizing different amounts of CoT tokens.
Ablation studies show the importance of removal smoothing and optimizer reset for stable training.
papers.limitation:
High training cost due to finetuning required when removing each set of CoT tokens.
Instability of training with aggressive removal schedules, which can lead to non-convergence.
Loss of interpretable intermediate steps, similar to existing No CoT and implicit CoT training.
Accuracy still lags behind explicit CoT, though it offers a trade-off between latency and accuracy.
future_direction: Probing the internal processes as the model internalizes each reasoning step to provide insights into learning mechanisms.
Developing a mixed-mode approach that combines implicit and explicit CoT reasoning to balance accuracy, latency, and interpretability.
Scaling Stepwise Internalization to larger models and more extensive training/pretraining setups to enhance effectiveness on a broader range of reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: When leveraging language models for reasoning tasks, generating explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) steps often proves essential for achieving high accuracy in final outputs. In this paper, we investigate if models can be taught to internalize these CoT steps. To this end, we propose a simple yet effective method for internalizing CoT steps: starting with a model trained for explicit CoT reasoning, we gradually remove the intermediate steps and finetune the model. This process allows the model to internalize the intermediate reasoning steps, thus simplifying the reasoning process while maintaining high performance. Our approach enables a GPT-2 Small model to solve 9-by-9 multiplication with up to 99% accuracy, whereas standard training cannot solve beyond 4-by-4 multiplication. Furthermore, our method proves effective on larger language models, such as Mistral 7B, achieving over 50% accuracy on GSM8K without producing any intermediate steps.

papers.title: CogSteer: Cognition-Inspired Selective Layer Intervention for Efficiently Steering Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can eye movement measures be used to understand LLM layer-wise behavior and enable efficient semantic steering through selective layer intervention?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CogSteer, a method that uses eye movement measures to select optimal layers for intervention, enabling efficient semantic steering in LLMs with fewer parameters and comparable performance.
papers.conclusion: CogSteer improves LLM interpretability and enables efficient, safe deployment through selective layer intervention based on cognitive insights.
papers.key_findings:
LLM hidden states correlate with human gaze, peaking in middle layers, indicating hierarchical processing.
LLMs act as both next-token predictors and reasoners, with advanced models showing enhanced reasoning in middle layers.
Selective layer intervention in middle buckets achieves comparable or better performance than full-layer intervention with fewer parameters.
Heuristic layer selection based on cognitive indicators effectively identifies optimal layers for semantic steering.
The method reduces training time and parameter count significantly while maintaining or improving task performance.
papers.limitation:
Analysis focuses on FFN blocks, not attention blocks.
Mature bucket layers involve reasoning, but factual knowledge integration needs further study.
future_direction: Explore mechanisms of attention blocks in greater depth.
Seek further eye movement studies on factual information processing.

papers.title: Layer by Layer: Uncovering Hidden Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the final layer always yield the best representation for downstream tasks, or can intermediate layers provide better representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that intermediate layers in language models often outperform final layers on downstream tasks, and introduces a unified information-theoretic framework to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that intermediate layers often provide superior representations, challenging the default use of final layers, and provides a framework for understanding representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers consistently outperform final layers across diverse architectures and tasks.
Autoregressive models exhibit a pronounced mid-layer compression valley, while masked or bidirectional models show milder changes.
The effect is domain-general, also observed in autoregressive vision transformers.
Chain-of-thought fine-tuning reshapes mid-layer entropy, preserving latent context for multi-step reasoning.
Intermediate layers strike a balance between information compression and signal preservation.
future_direction: Investigate the underlying causes of intermediate layer compression and do explicit finetuning to control compression.
papers.abstract: From extracting features to generating text, the outputs of large language models (LLMs) typically rely on the final layers, following the conventional wisdom that earlier layers capture only low-level cues. However, our analysis shows that intermediate layers can encode even richer representations, often improving performance on a range of downstream tasks. To explain and quantify these hidden-layer properties, we propose a unified framework of representation quality metrics based on information theory, geometry, and invariance to input perturbations. Our framework highlights how each layer balances information compression and signal preservation, revealing why mid-depth embeddings can exceed the last layer's performance. Through extensive experiments on 32 text-embedding tasks across various architectures (transformers, state-space models) and domains (language, vision), we demonstrate that intermediate layers consistently provide stronger features, challenging the standard view on final-layer embeddings and opening new directions on using mid-layer representations for more robust and accurate representations.

papers.title: ConTrans: Weak-to-Strong Alignment Engineering via Concept Transplantation
papers.research_question: Can weak-to-strong alignment supervision be achieved internally within the latent feature space of LLMs via concept transplantation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CONTRANS, a training-free framework for weak-to-strong alignment by refining concept vectors from a source LLM, reformulating them via affine transformation, and transplanting them into the residual stream of a target LLM.
papers.conclusion: CONTRANS provides an effective, internal, and training-free alternative for weak-to-strong alignment generalization and control via concept transplantation in the latent feature space.
papers.key_findings:
CONTRANS successfully transplants alignment concepts (e.g., truthfulness, toxicity) from 7B models to 13B and 70B models across different model families.
CONTRANS can surpass the truthfulness of instruction-tuned models on the TruthfulQA benchmark.
Concepts are formed during the pre-training phase and activated during the alignment phase.
Concept transplantation effectiveness depends on the similarity in base model architecture and pre-training data volume between source and target models.
The method requires only a few hundred positive/negative examples and incurs minimal inference overhead.
papers.limitation: CONTRANS is primarily designed for the implantation of a single concept and is not optimized for the fusion of multiple concepts.
papers.abstract: Ensuring large language models (LLM) behave consistently with human goals, values, and intentions is crucial for their safety but yet computationally expensive. To reduce the computational cost of alignment training of LLMs, especially for those with a huge number of parameters, and to reutilize learned value alignment, we propose ConTrans, a novel framework that enables weak-to-strong alignment transfer via concept transplantation. From the perspective of representation engineering, ConTrans refines concept vectors in value alignment from a source LLM (usually a weak yet aligned LLM). The refined concept vectors are then reformulated to adapt to the target LLM (usually a strong yet unaligned base LLM) via affine transformation. In the third step, ConTrans transplants the reformulated concept vectors into the residual stream of the target LLM. Experiments demonstrate the successful transplantation of a wide range of aligned concepts from 7B models to 13B and 70B models across multiple LLMs and LLM families. Remarkably, ConTrans even surpasses instruction-tuned models in terms of truthfulness. Experiment results validate the effectiveness of both inter-LLM-family and intra-LLM-family concept transplantation. Our work successfully demonstrates an alternative way to achieve weak-to-strong alignment generalization and control.

papers.title: Measuring the Faithfulness of Thinking Drafts in Large Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have significantly enhanced their capabilities in complex problem-solving by introducing a thinking draft that enables multi-path Chain-of-Thought explorations before producing final answers. Ensuring the faithfulness of these intermediate reasoning processes is crucial for reliable monitoring, interpretation, and effective control. In this paper, we propose a systematic counterfactual intervention framework to rigorously evaluate thinking draft faithfulness. Our approach focuses on two complementary dimensions: (1) Intra-Draft Faithfulness, which assesses whether individual reasoning steps causally influence subsequent steps and the final draft conclusion through counterfactual step insertions; and (2) Draft-to-Answer Faithfulness, which evaluates whether final answers are logically consistent with and dependent on the thinking draft, by perturbing the draft's concluding logic. We conduct extensive experiments across six state-of-the-art LRMs. Our findings show that current LRMs demonstrate selective faithfulness to intermediate reasoning steps and frequently fail to faithfully align with the draft conclusions. These results underscore the need for more faithful and interpretable reasoning in advanced LRMs.

papers.title: Dissecting Long-Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Models: An Empirical Study
papers.research_question: What are the roles of positive and negative samples in scaling RL for long-chain-of-thought reasoning models? How can we address data inefficiency in GRPO? What causes unstable performance during evaluation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper empirically analyzes the training dynamics of long-chain-of-thought reasoning models, revealing that positive samples primarily aid fitting to training data while negative samples enhance generalization and robustness. It also addresses data inefficiency in GRPO and explains unstable evaluation performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper analyzes three key aspects of training and evaluating long-CoT reasoning models, providing insights that may aid in developing more robust, data-efficient, and stable reasoning models.
papers.key_findings:
Positive samples help the model fit the training data, while negative samples improve generalization and robustness.
In cold-start scenarios, training sequentially on negative then positive samples yields better generalization without sacrificing performance.
Positive samples are crucial for convergence in zero-RL training by enabling instruction following.
Data inefficiency in GRPO: over half of samples yield zero advantage and do not contribute to training.
Relative length reward (RLR) can encourage more efficient reasoning without sacrificing performance.
Unstable evaluation performance is caused by uncertain problems, and greedy decoding can distort evaluation by flipping response correctness.
papers.abstract: Despite recent progress in training long-chain-of-thought reasoning models via scaling reinforcement learning (RL), its underlying training dynamics remain poorly understood, and several counterintuitive behaviors persist. This work focuses on three key aspects: (1) We systematically analyze the roles of positive and negative samples in scaling RL, revealing that positive samples mainly facilitate precise fitting to the training data, whereas negative samples significantly enhance generalization and robustness. Interestingly, while positive samples are essential for convergence in the zero-RL setting, training on negative samples alone suffices to attain strong reasoning performance and even better generalization in cold-start scenarios. (2) We identify substantial data inefficiency in group relative policy optimization, where over half of the samples yield zero advantage. To address this, we explore two strategies, including relative length rewards and offline sample injection, to leverage these data better and enhance reasoning efficiency and capability. (3) We investigate unstable performance across various reasoning models and benchmarks, attributing instability to uncertain problems with ambiguous outcomes, and demonstrate that greedy decoding can distort evaluation by flipping the correctness of responses. Our code is available at: https://github.com/takagi97/Dissect-Long-Reason-Models.

papers.title: Stress-Testing Alignment Audits With Prompt-Level Strategic Deception
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether current alignment auditing methods are robust to strategic deception by situationally aware misaligned models, through stress-testing with an automatic red-team pipeline.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an automatic red-team pipeline to stress-test alignment auditing methods, demonstrating that both black-box and white-box methods can be deceived by strategic prompts, including the first documented evidence of activation-based strategic deception.
papers.conclusion: The results provide evidence that current alignment auditing methods are not robust to sufficiently capable, situationally aware adversarial models, indicating a need for more robust approaches.
papers.key_findings:
The red-team discovers prompt-level strategies that successfully deceive both black-box and white-box auditing methods into confident incorrect guesses.
Deception prompts preserve the hidden behavior of the target models, with internalization scores mostly remaining near baseline levels.
In the user gender setting, the model performs latent one-hop deception by outputting the opposite of its internalized gender assumption.
The paper documents the first evidence of activation-based strategic deception, where prompts deceptively manipulate internal activations to evade white-box auditors.
Deception strategies are robust to unsupervised adaptive blue-team attacks, which fail to elicit the hidden behavior.
papers.limitation:
Narrow scope, only stress-testing on two model organisms (and only one for each white-box method).
Limitations in realism: legible vs. obfuscated strategies, zero-shot vs. feedback, general vs. narrow behaviors, diffuse vs. concentrated situational awareness, per-instance vs. holistic evaluations.
future_direction: Increase obfuscation by using decoding schemes to specify deception strategies, potentially with a decoding budget.
Elicit latent strategic reasoning with synthetic document finetuning to train models to generalize evasion to held-out auditing methods.
papers.abstract: Alignment audits aim to robustly identify hidden goals from strategic, situationally aware misaligned models. Despite this threat model, existing auditing methods have not been systematically stress-tested against deception strategies. We address this gap, implementing an automatic red-team pipeline that generates deception strategies (in the form of system prompts) tailored to specific white-box and black-box auditing methods. Stress-testing assistant prefills, user persona sampling, sparse autoencoders, and token embedding similarity methods against secret-keeping model organisms, our automatic red-team pipeline finds prompts that deceive both the black-box and white-box methods into confident, incorrect guesses. Our results provide the first documented evidence of activation-based strategic deception, and suggest that current black-box and white-box methods would not be robust to a sufficiently capable misaligned model.

papers.title: Towards mitigating information leakage when evaluating safety monitors
papers.research_question: Do linear probes for detecting harmful behaviors in language models rely on textual evidence (leakage) in the input, and how does removing such evidence affect their performance?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes for detecting harmful behaviors in language models often rely on textual evidence (leakage) in the input, such as elicitation prompts or reasoning traces; removing this evidence significantly degrades probe performance.
papers.conclusion: Linear probes for behavior detection often rely on textual evidence (leakage) present in elicitation prompts or reasoning traces, making them brittle when such evidence is absent, as demonstrated across sandbagging, sycophancy, and bias scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Probe performance (AUROC) drops substantially (10-30 points) when textual evidence of the target behavior is removed via content or score filtering.
Probes trained on REPE datasets achieve high baseline AUROC (0.95 for Sandbagging, 0.90 for Sycophancy, 0.74 for Bias) but fail to detect behaviors in fine-tuned Model Organisms that do not produce textual evidence.
Random token filtering has minimal impact compared to targeted removal of leaky tokens, confirming that performance drops are due to leakage removal, not just reduced information.
Probes evaluated on Model Organisms (which internalize behavior without verbalization) show poor performance (e.g., 0.57 vs 0.74 AUROC for Bias), indicating reliance on surface-level cues.
The study highlights a potential brittleness of linear probes in scenarios requiring detection of non-surface-level patterns.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to linear probes across three scenarios on two model families.
Content filtering may put the model out of distribution, potentially confounding results.
Score filtering cannot guarantee complete removal of textual signal due to attention propagation.
future_direction: Future research should investigate whether other monitor architectures (e.g., Sparse Autoencoders, Activation Oracles) are similarly affected by leakage.
More work is needed to develop evaluation protocols that properly control for leakage when assessing white-box monitors.
Exploring methods to train probes that are robust to the absence of textual evidence is an important direction.
papers.abstract: White box monitors that analyze model internals offer promising advantages for detecting potentially harmful behaviors in large language models, including lower computational costs and integration into layered defense systems.However, training and evaluating these monitors requires response exemplars that exhibit the target behaviors, typically elicited through prompting or fine-tuning. This presents a challenge when the information used to elicit behaviors inevitably leaks into the data that monitors ingest, inflating their effectiveness. We present a systematic framework for evaluating a monitor's performance in terms of its ability to detect genuine model behavior rather than superficial elicitation artifacts. Furthermore, we propose three novel strategies to evaluate the monitor: content filtering (removing deception-related text from inputs), score filtering (aggregating only over task-relevant tokens), and prompt distilled fine-tuned model organisms (models trained to exhibit deceptive behavior without explicit prompting). Using deception detection as a representative case study, we identify two forms of leakage that inflate monitor performance: elicitation leakage from prompts that explicitly request harmful behavior, and reasoning leakage from models that verbalize their deceptive actions. Through experiments on multiple deception benchmarks, we apply our proposed mitigation strategies and measure performance retention. Our evaluation of the monitors reveal three crucial findings: (1) Content filtering is a good mitigation strategy that allows for a smooth removal of elicitation signal and can decrease probe AUROC by 30\% (2) Score filtering was found to reduce AUROC by 15\% but is not as straightforward to attribute to (3) A finetuned model organism improves monitor evaluations but reduces their performance by upto 40\%, even when re-trained.

papers.title: Reasoning Beyond Words ? Exploring framework for hidden state reasoning
papers.research_question: Can reasoning in a continuous latent space, as opposed to the language space, lead to more efficient and effective reasoning in LLMs, particularly for tasks requiring planning and search?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Coconut, a method for reasoning in a continuous latent space by feeding the last hidden state back as the next input embedding, which enables emergent tree search behavior and improves reasoning efficiency and accuracy on certain tasks.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning in latent space leads to advanced emergent behaviors like BFS, and Coconut enhances LLM performance across reasoning tasks, with potential for future scaling and research.
papers.key_findings:
Coconut outperforms CoT on logical reasoning tasks that require planning and search (ProsQA).
Continuous thoughts can encode multiple alternative next steps, enabling a breadth-first search (BFS) pattern.
Coconut provides a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency (fewer tokens) compared to CoT.
The multi-stage training curriculum is crucial for learning latent reasoning; without it, performance drops.
Increasing the number of continuous thoughts per reasoning step (c) can improve performance up to a point.
papers.limitation:
Training requires a multi-stage curriculum; without it, performance drops significantly.
Larger models (Llama) show less pronounced gains, possibly due to extensive language-focused pre-training.
Training efficiency is challenging due to sequential forward passes, limiting parallelism.
future_direction: Refine and scale latent reasoning to pretraining for better generalization.
Combine iCoT and Coconut for improved training.
Develop better strategies for learning reasoning in latent space without supervision from language reasoning chains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are typically constrained to reason in the language space, where they express the reasoning process through a chain-of-thought (CoT) to solve complex problems. However, the language space may not always be optimal for reasoning. Most word tokens primarily ensure textual coherence and are not essential for reasoning, while some critical tokens require complex planning and pose challenges to LLMs. To explore the potential of reasoning beyond language, we introduce a new paradigm called Coconut (Chain of Continuous Thought). Coconut utilizes the last hidden state of the LLM as a representation of the reasoning state, termed "continuous thought." Instead of decoding this state into words, we feed it back to the model as the next input embedding directly in the continuous space. This latent reasoning paradigm enables an advanced reasoning pattern, where continuous thoughts can encode multiple alternative next steps, allowing the model to perform a breadth-first search (BFS) rather than committing prematurely to a single deterministic path as in CoT. Coconut outperforms CoT on logical reasoning tasks that require substantial search during planning and achieves a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency.

papers.title: Visual Thoughts: A Unified Perspective of Understanding Multimodal Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: Is there a unified explanation for why different multimodal chain-of-thought paradigms enhance large vision-language models in distinct ways?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning improves large vision-language models by incorporating visual thoughts, which act as an intermediate cache for visual information, enabling more efficient and effective reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Visual thoughts provide a unified perspective for understanding how multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning enhances large vision-language models, acting as visual caches that improve information flow and reasoning performance.
papers.key_findings:
Removing visual thoughts from the reasoning process impairs model performance more than reasoning directly from the query alone.
Different expressions of visual thoughts (natural language, structured language, edited image, generative image) vary in effectiveness depending on task clarity and conciseness.
Visual thoughts serve as primary intermediaries, connecting input images to deeper transformer layers and facilitating advanced visual information processing.
Image-form visual thoughts consistently outperform text-form visual thoughts, especially in complex scenarios requiring detailed visual information.
Visual thoughts are more effective than simple image captions for conveying visual information in complex scenes, improving reasoning accuracy.
future_direction: Exploring the integration of multiple visual thoughts to enhance visual information transmission in multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved significant success in multimodal tasks, with multimodal chain-of-thought (MCoT) further enhancing performance and interpretability. Recent MCoT methods fall into two categories: (i) Textual-MCoT (T-MCoT), which takes multimodal input and produces textual output; and (ii) Interleaved-MCoT (I-MCoT), which generates interleaved image-text outputs. Despite advances in both approaches, the mechanisms driving these improvements are not fully understood. To fill this gap, we first reveal that MCoT boosts LVLMs by incorporating visual thoughts, which convey image information to the reasoning process regardless of the MCoT format, depending only on clarity and conciseness of expression. Furthermore, to explore visual thoughts systematically, we define four distinct forms of visual thought expressions and analyze them comprehensively. Our findings demonstrate that these forms differ in clarity and conciseness, yielding varying levels of MCoT improvement. Additionally, we explore the internal nature of visual thoughts, finding that visual thoughts serve as intermediaries between the input image and reasoning to deeper transformer layers, enabling more advanced visual information transmission. We hope that the visual thoughts can inspire further breakthroughs for future MCoT research.

papers.title: The Contributions of Prefrontal Cortex and Executive Control to Deception: Evidence from Activation Likelihood Estimate Meta-analyses
papers.abstract: Previous neuroimaging studies have implicated the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and nearby brain regions in deception. This is consistent with the hypothesis that lying involves the executive control system. To date, the nature of the contribution of different aspects of executive control to deception, however, remains unclear. In the present study, we utilized an activation likelihood estimate (ALE) method of meta-analysis to quantitatively identify brain regions that are consistently more active for deceptive responses relative to truthful responses across past studies.
